papers.abstract: When a language model is trained to predict natural language sequences, its prediction at each moment depends on a representation of prior context. What kind of information about the prior context can language models retrieve? We tested whether language models could retrieve the exact words that occurred previously in a text. In our paradigm, language models (transformers and an LSTM) processed English text in which a list of nouns occurred twice. We operationalized retrieval as the reduction in surprisal from the first to the second list. We found that the transformers retrieved both the identity and ordering of nouns from the first list. Further, the transformers' retrieval was markedly enhanced when they were trained on a larger corpus and with greater model depth. Lastly, their ability to index prior tokens was dependent on learned attention patterns. In contrast, the LSTM exhibited less precise retrieval, which was limited to list-initial tokens and to short intervening texts. The LSTM's retrieval was not sensitive to the order of nouns and it improved when the list was semantically coherent. We conclude that transformers implemented something akin to a working memory system that could flexibly retrieve individual token representations across arbitrary delays; conversely, the LSTM maintained a coarser and more rapidly-decaying semantic gist of prior tokens, weighted toward the earliest items.

papers.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Build Predictions by Promoting Concepts in the Vocabulary Space
papers.research_question: How do transformer-based language models construct predictions, specifically through the operation of feed-forward network (FFN) layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that feed-forward network (FFN) layers in transformers operate by promoting interpretable concepts in the vocabulary space through sub-updates, and this understanding can be leveraged for controlling model predictions (e.g., reducing toxicity) and improving computational efficiency (e.g., early exiting).
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides a detailed understanding of the internal prediction process in transformer-based language models and suggests new research directions for interpretability, control, and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
FFN updates can be decomposed into sub-updates corresponding to value vectors, each promoting human-interpretable concepts in the vocabulary space.
FFN updates primarily work by promoting candidate tokens rather than eliminating them.
Value vectors across layers encode semantic, syntactic, and named entity concepts.
Activating a small set of non-toxic value vectors reduces toxicity in GPT2 generations by almost 50%.
Dominant sub-updates can signal saturation events, enabling an early exit rule that saves 20% of computation on average.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on FFN layers and did not analyze the interplay with other components like attention heads.
Value vectors might be compositional, but the paper only analyzes individual vectors.
The analysis is limited to decoder-based auto-regressive language models.
future_direction: Analyze the interplay between FFN layers and other components such as attention heads.
Improve the annotation protocol for concept identification by providing additional context.
Extend the analysis to other model architectures beyond decoder-based auto-regressive LMs.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are at the core of modern NLP, but their internal prediction construction process is opaque and largely not understood. In this work, we make a substantial step towards unveiling this underlying prediction process, by reverse-engineering the operation of the feed-forward network (FFN) layers, one of the building blocks of transformer models. We view the token representation as a changing distribution over the vocabulary, and the output from each FFN layer as an additive update to that distribution. Then, we analyze the FFN updates in the vocabulary space, showing that each update can be decomposed to sub-updates corresponding to single FFN parameter vectors, each promoting concepts that are often human-interpretable. We then leverage these findings for controlling LM predictions, where we reduce the toxicity of GPT2 by almost 50%, and for improving computation efficiency with a simple early exit rule, saving 20% of computation on average.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: Emergence and Effectiveness of Task Vectors in In-Context Learning: An Encoder Decoder Perspective
papers.research_question: How do transformers form task vectors during pretraining, and how does the quality of task encoding predict in-context learning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the task encoding-decoding framework and shows that transformers concurrently learn to encode latent tasks into separable representations and develop task-specific decoding algorithms during pretraining. It also introduces Task Decodability (TD) as a geometric measure that predicts in-context learning performance.
papers.conclusion: The task encoding-decoding framework provides a unifying perspective on how transformers perform in-context learning, with task decodability serving as a key predictor of performance.
papers.key_findings:
During training, task encoding and decoding emerge concurrently: as the model learns to separate representations by latent task, it also learns conditional decoding algorithms.
Task Decodability (TD) predicts ICL performance across tasks, model families, and scales.
Finetuning earlier layers improves task encoding and ICL performance more than finetuning later layers.
The quality of task encoding is causally related to ICL performance, as shown by activation patching interventions.
In-context examples, finetuning, and prompting all improve ICL performance by enhancing task encoding.
papers.limitation:
The experimental setup does not encompass tasks that require multi-step reasoning.
The TD metric requires careful design of task distribution to consist of semantically similar, confusing tasks.
future_direction: Extend the framework to tasks requiring multi-step reasoning.
Apply the findings to real-world tasks.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive transformers exhibit adaptive learning through in-context learning (ICL), which begs the question of how. Prior works have shown that transformers represent the ICL tasks as vectors in their representations. In this paper, we leverage the encoding-decoding framework to study how transformers form task vectors during pretraining and how their task encoding quality predicts ICL task performance. On synthetic ICL tasks, we analyze the training dynamics of a small transformer and report the coupled emergence of task encoding and decoding. As the model learns to encode different latent tasks (e.g., "Finding the first noun in a sentence.") into distinct, separable representations, it concurrently builds conditional decoding algorithms and improves its ICL performance. We validate this phenomenon across pretrained models of varying scales (Gemma-2 2B/9B/27B, Llama-3.1 8B/70B) and over the course of pretraining in OLMo-7B. Further, we demonstrate that the quality of task encoding inferred from representations predicts ICL performance, and that, surprisingly, finetuning the earlier layers can improve the task encoding and performance more than finetuning the latter layers. Our empirical insights shed light into better understanding the success and failure modes of large language models via their representations.

papers.title: Detecting and Characterizing Planning in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models plan ahead by selecting future tokens in advance, or do they improvise one token at a time? How can we distinguish planning from improvisation across models and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a formal, causally grounded definition of planning in LLMs, operationalized as a semi-automated detection pipeline using Future-Token Encoding (FTE) and Precursor Influence (PI) criteria. It applies this pipeline to show planning is not universal and instruction tuning refines existing planning behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Planning is not universal in language models, can be done poorly, and instruction tuning refines planning behavior rather than creating it from scratch.
papers.key_findings:
Planning is not universal: Gemma-2-2B solves a poem generation task through improvisation, unlike Claude 3.5 Haiku which was shown to plan.
On the MBPP code benchmark, Gemma-2-2B switches between planning and improvisation across similar tasks and even successive token predictions.
Instruction tuning refines existing planning behaviors in the base model rather than creating them from scratch.
The base model can plan, but sometimes plans incorrectly (e.g., competing plans or incorrect targets), leading to task failure.
The detection pipeline provides a reproducible and scalable foundation for mechanistic studies of planning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
SAEs were trained on the base model but applied to the instruction-tuned version, which may introduce representation mismatch.
Only MLP-attached SAEs were used, limiting the analysis to MLP features.
Polysemantic latents can satisfy the planning criteria but encode multiple concepts, making interpretation ambiguous.
The study is limited to Gemma-2-2B and the MBPP dataset and a poem task, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Understanding edge and 'can't say' cases to refine the definition and improve detection.
Automating offline detection by setting thresholds for degenerate outputs (e.g., repeating tokens, perplexity).
Extending the approach to online detection (detecting planning at test time without knowledge of future tokens).
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across a wide range of multi-step reasoning tasks. Recent work suggests that LLMs may perform planning - selecting a future target token in advance and generating intermediate tokens that lead towards it - rather than merely improvising one token at a time. However, existing studies assume fixed planning horizons and often focus on single prompts or narrow domains. To distinguish planning from improvisation across models and tasks, we present formal and causally grounded criteria for detecting planning and operationalize them as a semi-automated annotation pipeline. We apply this pipeline to both base and instruction-tuned Gemma-2-2B models on the MBPP code generation benchmark and a poem generation task where Claude 3.5 Haiku was previously shown to plan. Our findings show that planning is not universal: unlike Haiku, Gemma-2-2B solves the same poem generation task through improvisation, and on MBPP it switches between planning and improvisation across similar tasks and even successive token predictions. We further show that instruction tuning refines existing planning behaviors in the base model rather than creating them from scratch. Together, these studies provide a reproducible and scalable foundation for mechanistic studies of planning in LLMs.

papers.title: What Happens During the Loss Plateau? Understanding Abrupt Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: What common patterns manifest in the model's input-output behavior and internal representations during the extended loss plateau phase, and what critical changes precede the sudden shift towards higher performance?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies that during the loss plateau in Transformer training, models develop a partial solution, exhibit repetition bias and internal representation collapse, and that the slow learning of optimal attention maps is a key bottleneck driving these dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies repetition bias and representation collapse as key characteristics of early-phase implicit biases in Transformer training, closely connected to the loss plateau, and suggests a 'search' over sequence tokens as a possible cause.
papers.key_findings:
During the initial loss plateau, the model often learns a partial solution, correctly predicting a subset of easier tokens while failing on more complex parts.
A strong repetition bias appears in model outputs during the plateau, quantified by repetition frequency and sequence entropy.
Internal representation collapse occurs where hidden states for different tokens become nearly parallel (high cosine similarity).
Gradual learning of the optimal attention pattern commences during the plateau and precedes the sudden loss drop; intervening on attention maps alters plateau duration and degenerate behaviors.
The phenomena of repetition bias and representation collapse are also observed in the early pre-training stages of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.
future_direction: Understanding why behaviors such as representation collapse exist during early time training.
Rigorous theoretical validation of the 'search' hypothesis and how it connects to task complexity.
papers.abstract: Training Transformers on algorithmic tasks frequently demonstrates an intriguing abrupt learning phenomenon: an extended performance plateau followed by a sudden, sharp improvement. This work investigates the underlying mechanisms for such dynamics, primarily in shallow Transformers. We reveal that during the plateau, the model often develops an interpretable partial solution while simultaneously exhibiting a strong repetition bias in their outputs. This output degeneracy is accompanied by internal representation collapse, where hidden states across different tokens become nearly parallel. We further identify the slow learning of optimal attention maps as a key bottleneck. Hidden progress in attention configuration during the plateau precedes the eventual rapid convergence, and directly intervening on attention significantly alters plateau duration and the severity of repetition bias and representational collapse. We validate that these identified phenomena-repetition bias and representation collapse-are not artifacts of toy setups but also manifest in the early pre-training stage of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.

papers.title: Constrained belief updates explain geometric structures in transformer representations
papers.research_question: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? How do transformers resolve the conflict between optimal Bayesian belief updating (a recursive process) and their parallelized, attention-driven architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating—a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. It explains why specific intermediate geometric structures emerge in transformer representations.
papers.conclusion: The geometric structures in transformer representations are a mathematical signature of how architectural constraints warp optimal Bayesian inference, revealing a precise interplay between theoretical necessity and implementation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating due to architectural constraints, bending optimal Bayesian inference into attention's parallelizable form.
The attention mechanism in the first layer implements a spectral algorithm that builds constrained beliefs, with attention weights approximating the decay of influence via eigenvalues of the data-generating transition matrix.
Intermediate representations (after attention) are fractals matching the constrained belief geometry, while final representations (after MLP) match the full, unconstrained belief geometry.
The attention pattern, OV vectors, and token embeddings can be theoretically predicted from the constrained belief updating equations.
For negative eigenvalues in the transition matrix (oscillatory dynamics), multiple attention heads are required to capture the full update pattern due to the non-negativity constraint of attention.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is conducted on a tractable family of hidden Markov models (Mess3), which is a simplified setting.
As the HMM parameter α moves away from a central range, deviations between predicted and actual representations increase, and a complete characterization of these deviations remains for future work.
future_direction: A complete characterization of how deviations between predicted and actual representations scale with the HMM parameter α.
Applying the methodology to more complex cases, such as large language models trained on natural text, where the same tension between architecture and optimal inference is anticipated.
papers.abstract: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? In this work, we provide evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating -- a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. We integrate the model-agnostic theory of optimal prediction with mechanistic interpretability to analyze transformers trained on a tractable family of hidden Markov models that generate rich geometric patterns in neural activations. Our primary analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, revealing how the first attention layer implements these constrained updates, with extensions to multi-layer architectures demonstrating how subsequent layers refine these representations. We find that attention carries out an algorithm with a natural interpretation in the probability simplex, and create representations with distinctive geometric structure. We show how both the algorithmic behavior and the underlying geometry of these representations can be theoretically predicted in detail -- including the attention pattern, OV-vectors, and embedding vectors -- by modifying the equations for optimal future token predictions to account for the architectural constraints of attention. Our approach provides a principled lens on how architectural constraints shape the implementation of optimal prediction, revealing why transformers develop specific intermediate geometric structures.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Jump to Conclusions: Short-Cutting Transformers With Linear Transformations
papers.research_question: Is there a more accurate way to cast hidden representations into final representation substitutes than interpreting them as they are (identity mapping)?
papers.core_contribution: A simple method using linear transformations to cast hidden representations to final-layer substitutes, which improves interpretability and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Linear mappings provide a simple and effective way to enhance the utilization of hidden representations for interpretability and efficiency, revealing linear structure in transformer components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear mappings (mat) consistently outperform identity mapping (id) in approximating future hidden representations and final predictions.
The method allows accurate prediction estimation from early layers, showing that models often predict the final output early.
The learned linear mappings generalize well across different model scales and data distributions.
When applied to early exiting, the method saves additional layers (e.g., 7.9% for GPT-2, 5.4% for BERT) while retaining 95% accuracy.
Attention sub-modules are the most tolerant to linear approximation compared to FFN and layer normalization.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on linear transformations, leaving affine or non-linear transformations for future work.
Does not elucidate the reason for the linear structure observed in transformer inference.
Only considers post-hoc interpretability (analyzing trained models without changing weights).
Experiments are conducted only on English data.
future_direction: Exploring affine or non-linear transformations for casting hidden representations.
Integrating linear mappings into model training rather than only post-hoc analysis.
Breaking the computation into parallel tasks to improve efficiency.
Comparing the method with other approaches like Belrose et al. (2023).
Investigating the reasons for the linear structure in transformer components.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models create hidden representations of their inputs at every layer, but only use final-layer representations for prediction. This obscures the internal decision-making process of the model and the utility of its intermediate representations. One way to elucidate this is to cast the hidden representations as final representations, bypassing the transformer computation in-between. In this work, we suggest a simple method for such casting, using linear transformations. This approximation far exceeds the prevailing practice of inspecting hidden representations from all layers, in the space of the final layer. Moreover, in the context of language modeling, our method produces more accurate predictions from hidden layers, across various model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This allows "peeking" into intermediate representations, showing that GPT-2 and BERT often predict the final output already in early layers. We then demonstrate the practicality of our method to recent early exit strategies, showing that when aiming, for example, at retention of 95% accuracy, our approach saves additional 7.9% layers for GPT-2 and 5.4% layers for BERT. Last, we extend our method to linearly approximate sub-modules, finding that attention is most tolerant to this change. Our code and learned mappings are publicly available at https://github.com/sashayd/mat.

papers.title: Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent can transformers use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') to perform hidden computation and solve algorithmic tasks they cannot solve without intermediate tokens, and under what conditions does this occur?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can use meaningless filler tokens to solve hard algorithmic tasks they fail at without intermediate tokens, showing additional tokens provide computational benefits independent of token meaning, but learning to use filler tokens requires specific, dense supervision.
papers.conclusion: For certain parallelizable problems, transformers achieve improved performance with filler tokens instead of chain-of-thought tokens, meaning intermediate tokens can be used purely for computational capacity rather than faithful serial reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve perfect accuracy on 3SUM and high accuracy on 2SUM-Transform with filler tokens, while failing without them.
The performance gap between filler and no-filler settings increases with problem complexity (input length and dimension).
Filler token representations encode hidden, task-relevant computation, as shown by fine-tuning experiments.
Learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires training on parallelizable chain-of-thought data; instance-adaptive CoT data does not transfer.
Filler tokens extend transformer expressive power within the complexity class TC0, enabling solution of problems with deep quantifier nesting.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which token-parallelizable, TC0 algorithmic problems arise in natural language contexts.

Investigate whether natural-language text provides adequate supervision for filler-token computation, providing parallelizable supervision rather than non-parallelizable, instance-adaptive chains of thought.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought responses from language models improve performance across most benchmarks. However, it remains unclear to what extent these performance gains can be attributed to human-like task decomposition or simply the greater computation that additional tokens allow. We show that transformers can use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') in place of a chain of thought to solve two hard algorithmic tasks they could not solve when responding without intermediate tokens. However, we find empirically that learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires specific, dense supervision to converge. We also provide a theoretical characterization of the class of problems where filler tokens are useful in terms of the quantifier depth of a first-order formula. For problems satisfying this characterization, chain-of-thought tokens need not provide information about the intermediate computational steps involved in multi-token computations. In summary, our results show that additional tokens can provide computational benefits independent of token choice. The fact that intermediate tokens can act as filler tokens raises concerns about large language models engaging in unauditable, hidden computations that are increasingly detached from the observed chain-of-thought tokens.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Understanding and Enhancing the Planning Capability of Language Models via Multi-Token Prediction
papers.research_question: How does Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) affect the learning of transitive relations in language models for planning tasks, and how can we enhance it?
papers.core_contribution: Theoretical analysis reveals that MTP enables learning of transitive reachability beyond observed paths, and two enhancements—Next-Token Injection (NTI) and a Transformer-based transfer layer—are proposed to improve planning capability.
papers.conclusion: These findings deepen our understanding of how Transformers with MTP learn in complex planning tasks and provide practical strategies to overcome the transitivity bottleneck, paving the way toward structurally aware and general-purpose planning models.
papers.key_findings:
MTP enables the model to learn transitive reachability relations not directly observed in training data.
The transfer layer in MTP approximates the adjacency matrix of the underlying graph.
Next-Token Injection (NTI) stabilizes training and improves accuracy by injecting true next-token information.
Replacing the linear transfer layer with a Transformer-based layer enhances modeling of multi-hop relations.
The proposed enhancements significantly improve path-planning accuracy, especially on higher-degree (more complex) test paths.
papers.limitation:
Spurious adjacency may be introduced into the backbone matrix when learning transitive reachability, which is mechanically difficult to avoid.
When the number of nodes exceeds the embedding capacity, supervision signals from different tokens may conflict, limiting the model's ability to encode structural patterns.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved impressive performance across diverse tasks but continue to struggle with learning transitive relations, a cornerstone for complex planning. To address this issue, we investigate the Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) paradigm and its impact to transitive relation learning. We theoretically analyze the MTP paradigm using a Transformer architecture composed of a shared output head and a transfer layer. Our analysis reveals that the transfer layer gradually learns the multi-step adjacency information, which in turn enables the backbone model to capture unobserved transitive reachability relations beyond those directly present in the training data, albeit with some inevitable noise in adjacency estimation. Building on this foundation, we propose two strategies to enhance the transfer layer and overall learning quality: Next-Token Injection (NTI) and a Transformer-based transfer layer. Our experiments on both synthetic graphs and the Blocksworld planning benchmark validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate that the improvements significantly enhance the model's path-planning capability. These findings deepen our understanding of how Transformers with MTP learn in complex planning tasks, and provide practical strategies to overcome the transitivity bottleneck, paving the way toward structurally aware and general-purpose planning models.

papers.title: minicons: Enabling Flexible Behavioral and Representational Analyses of Transformer Language Models
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces minicons, an open-source library that provides a standard API for behavioral and representational analyses of transformer language models, facilitating efficient extraction of word/sentence probabilities and contextualized embeddings.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents minicons, a utility tool for analyzing transformer language models, and demonstrates its use in two case studies, showing its potential for facilitating behavioral and representational analyses.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's knowledge of linguistic acceptability emerges at different rates for different phenomena, with some phenomena showing signs of forgetting during training.
On zero-shot abductive reasoning, most models perform near chance, with ALBERT-xxlarge-v2 achieving the best accuracy (0.61) despite being smaller than other models.
Performance on abductive reasoning scales linearly with the logarithm of the number of parameters (R²=0.48), suggesting that scaling alone is unlikely to reach state-of-the-art performance.
future_direction: Integrate newer utility functions into the library and develop detailed tutorials for users.
papers.abstract: We present minicons, an open source library that provides a standard API for researchers interested in conducting behavioral and representational analyses of transformer-based language models (LMs). Specifically, minicons enables researchers to apply analysis methods at two levels: (1) at the prediction level -- by providing functions to efficiently extract word/sentence level probabilities; and (2) at the representational level -- by also facilitating efficient extraction of word/phrase level vectors from one or more layers. In this paper, we describe the library and apply it to two motivating case studies: One focusing on the learning dynamics of the BERT architecture on relative grammatical judgments, and the other on benchmarking 23 different LMs on zero-shot abductive reasoning. minicons is available at https://github.com/kanishkamisra/minicons

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of Contextual Representation Flow in State-Space and Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: How does contextual information flow across layers in State Space Models (SSMs) and Transformer-Based Models (TBMs)?
papers.core_contribution: TBMs rapidly homogenize token representations early with diversity reemerging later, while SSMs preserve token uniqueness early but converge to homogenization deeper. Oversmoothing in TBMs stems from architectural design, whereas in SSMs it arises mainly from training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: TBMs and SSMs exhibit opposing oversmoothing trajectories: TBMs homogenize early then recover, while SSMs preserve early token uniqueness but converge to homogenization deeper.
papers.key_findings:
TBMs exhibit stable token evolution until a sharp final-layer shift, while SSMs show varied directional changes that converge in later layers.
TBMs collapse token distinctions early and recover diversity late, while SSMs maintain token uniqueness longer.
Oversmoothing in TBMs is an intrinsic architectural property, while in SSMs it is primarily a consequence of training.
Task-relevant representations peak in intermediate layers for both architectures, with SSMs having a smaller accuracy gap to the final layer than TBMs.
Despite stable representation evolution across context lengths, probing accuracy decreases as context length increases, indicating capacity limitations.
papers.limitation:
Cosine similarity is sensitive to parameterizations, biased by skip connections, and captures only local directional changes.
Findings are limited to the specific tasks (MDQA, KVPR) and models examined, which may limit generality.
future_direction: Extend the framework to multimodal domains such as video or speech.
Integrate similarity measures into the training loop for adaptive regularization schemes.
Explore hybrid architectures that combine the local retention of SSMs with the global reconfiguration capacity of TBMs.
papers.abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have recently emerged as efficient alternatives to Transformer-Based Models (TBMs) for long-sequence processing with linear scaling, yet how contextual information flows across layers in these architectures remains understudied. We present the first unified, token- and layer-wise analysis of representation propagation in SSMs and TBMs. Using centered kernel alignment, variance-based metrics, and probing, we characterize how representations evolve within and across layers. We find a key divergence: TBMs rapidly homogenize token representations, with diversity reemerging only in later layers, while SSMs preserve token uniqueness early but converge to homogenization deeper. Theoretical analysis and parameter randomization further reveal that oversmoothing in TBMs stems from architectural design, whereas in SSMs, it arises mainly from training dynamics. These insights clarify the inductive biases of both architectures and inform future model and training designs for long-context reasoning.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Reinforcement Learning Using Attention Augmented Agents
papers.research_question: How can an attention mechanism be used to create interpretable reinforcement learning agents while maintaining competitive performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a soft attention model for RL that provides interpretability through attention maps while achieving competitive performance on ATARI games.
papers.conclusion: The attention mechanism provides interpretability and competitive performance, and the agent learns meaningful attention strategies for decision making.
papers.key_findings:
The agent learns to attend to task-relevant objects like the player, enemies, and score.
The agent can react appropriately to novel, unseen configurations of the environment.
The agent performs forward planning/scanning by attending to possible future trajectories.
The agent uses 'trip wires' (attention at strategic points) to trigger specific actions.
The agent's queries separate 'what' (content) and 'where' (spatial) information.
papers.abstract: Inspired by recent work in attention models for image captioning and question answering, we present a soft attention model for the reinforcement learning domain. This model uses a soft, top-down attention mechanism to create a bottleneck in the agent, forcing it to focus on task-relevant information by sequentially querying its view of the environment. The output of the attention mechanism allows direct observation of the information used by the agent to select its actions, enabling easier interpretation of this model than of traditional models. We analyze different strategies that the agents learn and show that a handful of strategies arise repeatedly across different games. We also show that the model learns to query separately about space and content (`where' vs. `what'). We demonstrate that an agent using this mechanism can achieve performance competitive with state-of-the-art models on ATARI tasks while still being interpretable.

papers.title: How Do Neural Sequence Models Generalize? Local and Global Context Cues for Out-of-Distribution Prediction
papers.research_question: After a neural sequence model encounters an unexpected token, can its behavior be predicted? The paper investigates how neural language models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts with conflicting local and global information.
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts by interpolating between local and global context predictions, and this interpolation can be modulated by noise-based regularization.
papers.conclusion: When neural sequence models are exposed to out-of-distribution contexts with conflicting local and global information, their behavior can be predicted and is best approximated by a log-linear interpolation of local and global predictors, with the weighting sometimes controllable by noise-based regularization.
papers.key_findings:
Neural LM predictions in surprising contexts are well approximated by a log-linear combination of local and global predictive distributions.
The relative strength of local versus global generalization varies across languages (e.g., local works better for English, global for Finnish and Chinese).
Input token noise (random substitution) encourages global generalization, while history representation noise (dropout) encourages local generalization.
A theoretical analysis shows that interpolation behavior arises in regularized log-linear models with separate local and global features.
papers.limitation: The theoretical explanation relies on a feature function that may not realistically represent deep network features, makes strong assumptions about feature predictive power, and becomes vacuous for certain parameter values.
future_direction: Explaining data-dependent aspects of the local-global trade-off, especially cross-linguistic differences not explained by typology.
Determining if architectural improvements can more effectively target specific kinds of structured generalization.
papers.abstract: After a neural sequence model encounters an unexpected token, can its behavior be predicted? We show that RNN and transformer language models exhibit structured, consistent generalization in out-of-distribution contexts. We begin by introducing two idealized models of generalization in next-word prediction: a local context model in which generalization is consistent with the last word observed, and a global context model in which generalization is consistent with the global structure of the input. In experiments in English, Finnish, Mandarin, and random regular languages, we demonstrate that neural language models interpolate between these two forms of generalization: their predictions are well-approximated by a log-linear combination of local and global predictive distributions. We then show that, in some languages, noise mediates the two forms of generalization: noise applied to input tokens encourages global generalization, while noise in history representations encourages local generalization. Finally, we offer a preliminary theoretical explanation of these results by proving that the observed interpolation behavior is expected in log-linear models with a particular feature correlation structure. These results help explain the effectiveness of two popular regularization schemes and show that aspects of sequence model generalization can be understood and controlled.

papers.title: Unlocking Compositional Generalization in Pre-trained Models Using Intermediate Representations
papers.research_question: How can intermediate representations be designed to improve compositional generalization in pre-trained seq2seq models?
papers.core_contribution: Intermediate representations designed to increase structural correspondence with natural language significantly improve compositional generalization in pre-trained seq2seq models, and these representations synergize with pre-training.
papers.conclusion: Intermediate representations are a simple yet effective strategy for improving compositional generalization in pre-trained seq2seq models, and they work synergistically with pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
Reversible intermediate representations (RIR) that group conjuncts, shorten relations, and add brackets improve compositional generalization on CFQ and SCAN.
Lossy intermediate representations (LIR) that anonymize entities and variables further improve performance when combined with RIR, especially on text-to-SQL datasets.
The benefits of intermediate representations are synergistic with pre-training; they yield larger gains when applied to pre-trained models than when applied to models without pre-training.
The best combinations of intermediate representations and pre-trained models achieve state-of-the-art results on CFQ and text-to-SQL template splits.
Intermediate representations maintain performance on i.i.d. splits while providing large gains on compositional splits.
papers.limitation: Designing intermediate representations requires customization for each new formalism, which involves manual work.
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models are prevalent in semantic parsing, but have been found to struggle at out-of-distribution compositional generalization. While specialized model architectures and pre-training of seq2seq models have been proposed to address this issue, the former often comes at the cost of generality and the latter only shows limited success. In this paper, we study the impact of intermediate representations on compositional generalization in pre-trained seq2seq models, without changing the model architecture at all, and identify key aspects for designing effective representations. Instead of training to directly map natural language to an executable form, we map to a reversible or lossy intermediate representation that has stronger structural correspondence with natural language. The combination of our proposed intermediate representations and pre-trained models is surprisingly effective, where the best combinations obtain a new state-of-the-art on CFQ (+14.8 accuracy points) and on the template-splits of three text-to-SQL datasets (+15.0 to +19.4 accuracy points). This work highlights that intermediate representations provide an important and potentially overlooked degree of freedom for improving the compositional generalization abilities of pre-trained seq2seq models.

papers.title: Transformers as Multi-task Learners: Decoupling Features in Hidden Markov Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformers achieve multi-task generalization? Specifically, what are the layerwise mechanisms by which they represent and process sequential information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers learn local features in lower layers and decoupled, temporally disentangled features in upper layers when modeling Hidden Markov Models, and provides theoretical constructions that align with these observations.
papers.conclusion: This work advances theoretical and empirical understanding of how Transformers achieve strong generalization across sequence learning tasks, showing they transition from local feature learning in lower layers to decoupled representations in upper layers, providing a principled explanation for their expressiveness and efficiency in multi-task and in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Well-trained Transformers achieve high accuracy under in-context learning on HMMs, with performance improving as more input-output examples are provided or as sequence length increases.
Lower layers of Transformers focus on learning local representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens.
Upper layers develop decoupled, temporally disentangled representations that are less tied to specific input positions and encode higher-level abstractions.
Transformers gradually recognize task identity across layers, with hidden state identification occurring earlier than task identification, indicating a layerwise processing hierarchy.
The theoretical construction demonstrates that Transformers can approximate low-rank HMMs using a fixed-length memory structure, enabling effective in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Analysis is limited to Hidden Markov Models and may not generalize to more complex settings.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more general assumptions and more complex model settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer based models have shown remarkable capabilities in sequence learning across a wide range of tasks, often performing well on specific task by leveraging input-output examples. Despite their empirical success, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. In this work, we investigate the layerwise behavior of Transformers to uncover the mechanisms underlying their multi-task generalization ability. Taking explorations on a typical sequence model, i.e, Hidden Markov Models, which are fundamental to many language tasks, we observe that: first, lower layers of Transformers focus on extracting feature representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens; second, on the upper layers, features become decoupled, exhibiting a high degree of time disentanglement. Building on these empirical insights, we provide theoretical analysis for the expressiveness power of Transformers. Our explicit constructions align closely with empirical observations, providing theoretical support for the Transformer's effectiveness and efficiency on sequence learning across diverse tasks.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: From Memories to Maps: Mechanisms of In-Context Reinforcement Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: How does episodic memory serve as a computational substrate for rapid in-context reinforcement learning in transformers, and what mechanisms emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained for in-context reinforcement learning develop mechanisms that use memory tokens to cache intermediate computations, enabling rapid planning without standard model-free or model-based RL algorithms.
papers.conclusion: Memory serves as a computational resource in transformers, caching computations to support flexible behavior, and these mechanisms resemble those in the brain's hippocampal-entorhinal system.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can rapidly learn to solve novel planning tasks after minimal in-context experience.
The model develops structured representations aligned with environment geometry through in-context structure learning.
Representations are aligned across environments with shared topology, indicating cross-context alignment.
The learned RL strategy is not standard model-free or model-based planning; instead, it relies on caching intermediate computations in memory tokens.
The model's representations and memory recall patterns resemble computations in the hippocampal-entorhinal system.
papers.limitation: The kernel alignment measure is imperfect for quantifying representation structure, especially in tree mazes.
papers.abstract: Humans and animals show remarkable learning efficiency, adapting to new environments with minimal experience. This capability is not well captured by standard reinforcement learning algorithms that rely on incremental value updates. Rapid adaptation likely depends on episodic memory -- the ability to retrieve specific past experiences to guide decisions in novel contexts. Transformers provide a useful setting for studying these questions because of their ability to learn rapidly in-context and because their key-value architecture resembles episodic memory systems in the brain. We train a transformer to in-context reinforcement learn in a distribution of planning tasks inspired by rodent behavior. We then characterize the learning algorithms that emerge in the model. We first find that representation learning is supported by in-context structure learning and cross-context alignment, where representations are aligned across environments with different sensory stimuli. We next demonstrate that the reinforcement learning strategies developed by the model are not interpretable as standard model-free or model-based planning. Instead, we show that in-context reinforcement learning is supported by caching intermediate computations within the model's memory tokens, which are then accessed at decision time. Overall, we find that memory may serve as a computational resource, storing both raw experience and cached computations to support flexible behavior. Furthermore, the representations developed in the model resemble computations associated with the hippocampal-entorhinal system in the brain, suggesting that our findings may be relevant for natural cognition. Taken together, our work offers a mechanistic hypothesis for the rapid adaptation that underlies in-context learning in artificial and natural settings.

papers.title: Modeling Language as a Sequence of Thoughts
papers.research_question: Can a recurrent transformer that models language at both token and sentence-level thought states improve data and parameter efficiency and generalization compared to standard transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Thought Gestalt model, a recurrent transformer that learns sentence-level representations end-to-end via next-token prediction, leading to improved data and parameter efficiency and better relational generalization compared to standard transformers.
papers.conclusion: The TG model demonstrates that learning latent sentence representations end-to-end via next-token prediction leads to more data-efficient and parameter-efficient language modeling and mitigates the reversal curse.
papers.key_findings:
TG achieves 2-4% lower test perplexity than GPT-2 across dataset sizes, corresponding to 5-8% more data efficiency.
TG requires 33-42% fewer parameters to match GPT-2's loss.
TG improves generalization on the in-context reversal curse probe, reducing the directional bias.
Ablations show that the working memory and gradient flow through memory are essential for TG's performance.
Other baselines (sentence boundary bias, fixed token-span recurrence, gist masking) do not match TG's performance.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models can generate strikingly natural text by modeling language as a sequence of tokens, but by relying primarily on surface-level co-occurrence statistics they fail to form globally consistent latent representations of entities and events, which contributes to poor relational generalization (the reversal curse), contextualization errors, and data inefficiency. Cognitive science, by contrast, shows that human comprehension converts linguistic input into compact, event-like representations that persist in memory while verbatim form is short-lived. Motivated by these findings, we introduce the Thought Gestalt (TG) model, a recurrent transformer that models language at two levels of abstraction: tokens and sentence-level "thought" states. TG generates one sentence at a time while cross-attending to a working memory of prior sentence representations. Token and sentence representations are generated using a shared stack of transformer blocks and trained with a single objective, next-token prediction loss. By retaining the computation graph of sentence representations written to working memory, gradients from future token losses flow backward through cross-attention to optimize the parameters that generate earlier sentence vectors. In scaling experiments, TG consistently improves data and parameter efficiency compared to matched GPT-2 runs and other baselines, with scaling fits indicating GPT-2 requires ~5-8% more data and ~33-42% more parameters to match TG's test loss. TG also reduces errors in relational-direction generalization on a father-son reversal curse probe.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Future Lens: Anticipating Subsequent Tokens from a Single Hidden State
papers.research_question: To what extent can we extract information about future tokens (beyond the next token) from a single hidden state representation in a transformer language model?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden states in transformer language models encode information about future tokens, and a learned prompt intervention method can effectively decode this information, enabling a new visualization tool called Future Lens.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states in transformers encode information about future tokens, and the proposed methods, especially learned prompt intervention, can decode this information, providing a new tool for interpreting model internals.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden states encode information about future tokens beyond the next token.
A learned prompt intervention method is the most effective at extracting future token information from hidden states.
Predictive accuracy for future tokens peaks at middle layers, unlike next-token prediction which peaks at the last layer.
The Future Lens tool visualizes the future tokens predicted by each hidden state across layers.
The accuracy of predicting future tokens correlates with the model's confidence in its next token prediction.
papers.limitation:
