Experiments were conducted only on English data with a relatively small sample size (100,000 tokens) compared to the full training data of GPT-J-6B.
Experiments were only conducted on GPT-J-6B; testing on other LLMs would be more comprehensive.
There are no prior baselines for decoding far future tokens, so the comparison is limited to bigram and linear models.
Experiments only tested up to 4 tokens in the future (N=0,1,2,3); scaling to more tokens is an open question.
future_direction: Testing the methods on other large language models.
Scaling the experiments to predict more tokens into the future.
Comparing with other architectures like Recurrent Neural Networks or Non-Autoregressive models as baselines.
papers.abstract: We conjecture that hidden state vectors corresponding to individual input tokens encode information sufficient to accurately predict several tokens ahead. More concretely, in this paper we ask: Given a hidden (internal) representation of a single token at position $t$ in an input, can we reliably anticipate the tokens that will appear at positions $\geq t + 2$? To test this, we measure linear approximation and causal intervention methods in GPT-J-6B to evaluate the degree to which individual hidden states in the network contain signal rich enough to predict future hidden states and, ultimately, token outputs. We find that, at some layers, we can approximate a model's output with more than 48% accuracy with respect to its prediction of subsequent tokens through a single hidden state. Finally we present a "Future Lens" visualization that uses these methods to create a new view of transformer states.

papers.title: (How) Do Language Models Track State?
papers.research_question: How do language models track the unobserved state of an evolving world? The paper studies this using permutation composition as a model system.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformer LMs learn one of two interpretable state-tracking mechanisms for permutation composition (associative algorithm or parity-associative algorithm), and the emergence of these mechanisms can be predicted and controlled via training interventions.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn either AA or PAA for state tracking; AA leads to better generalization and faster convergence, and the mechanism choice can be influenced by architecture and training.
papers.key_findings:
LMs learn either an associative algorithm (AA) or a parity-associative algorithm (PAA) for state tracking in permutation composition.
AA closely resembles the associative scan construction from theoretical work, while PAA uses a parity heuristic followed by an associative scan.
AA-type models generalize better and converge faster than PAA-type models.
The choice between AA and PAA is stochastic but can be influenced by model architecture, initialization, and intermediate training tasks.
No evidence is found for step-by-step simulation or fully parallel composition, despite their theoretical implementability.
papers.limitation:
It is unclear whether the mechanisms identified for permutation composition generalize to other state tracking tasks.
Experiments are conducted on small-scale models, limiting generalizability to larger models.
future_direction: Investigate whether the identified mechanisms generalize to other state tracking tasks.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models (LMs) exhibit behaviors -- from storytelling to code generation -- that seem to require tracking the unobserved state of an evolving world. How do they do this? We study state tracking in LMs trained or fine-tuned to compose permutations (i.e., to compute the order of a set of objects after a sequence of swaps). Despite the simple algebraic structure of this problem, many other tasks (e.g., simulation of finite automata and evaluation of boolean expressions) can be reduced to permutation composition, making it a natural model for state tracking in general. We show that LMs consistently learn one of two state tracking mechanisms for this task. The first closely resembles the "associative scan" construction used in recent theoretical work by Liu et al. (2023) and Merrill et al. (2024). The second uses an easy-to-compute feature (permutation parity) to partially prune the space of outputs, and then refines this with an associative scan. LMs that learn the former algorithm tend to generalize better and converge faster, and we show how to steer LMs toward one or the other with intermediate training tasks that encourage or suppress the heuristics. Our results demonstrate that transformer LMs, whether pre-trained or fine-tuned, can learn to implement efficient and interpretable state-tracking mechanisms, and the emergence of these mechanisms can be predicted and controlled.

papers.title: How Do Neural Sequence Models Generalize? Local and Global Cues for Out-of-Distribution Prediction
papers.research_question: How do neural sequence models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts when local and global context cues conflict?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neural language models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts by interpolating between local and global context cues, and that noise-based regularization can control this interpolation.
papers.conclusion: Neural sequence models' out-of-distribution generalization can be predicted by a log-linear interpolation of local and global context cues, and the weighting can be controlled by noise-based regularization.
papers.key_findings:
Neural language models' out-of-distribution predictions are well approximated by a log-linear interpolation of local and global context models.
Generalization behavior varies across languages: local context model fits well for regular languages and English, while global context model fits better for Finnish and Chinese.
Noise during training modulates the interpolation: input token substitution encourages global generalization, while hidden state dropout encourages local generalization.
Log-linear interpolation consistently outperforms linear interpolation in predicting model behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows that interpolation behavior arises in regularized log-linear models with separate local and global features.
papers.limitation: The theoretical explanation relies on a feature function that may not realistically represent deep network features, makes strong assumptions about feature predictive power, and becomes vacuous for certain parameter values.
future_direction: Explaining data-dependent aspects of the local-global trade-off, especially cross-linguistic differences.
Determining whether architectural improvements can more effectively target specific kinds of structured generalization.
papers.abstract: After a neural sequence model encounters an unexpected token, can its behavior be predicted? We show that RNN and transformer language models exhibit structured, consistent generalization in out-of-distribution contexts. We begin by introducing two idealized models of generalization in next-word prediction: a local context model in which generalization is consistent with the last word observed, and a global context model in which generalization is consistent with the global structure of the input. In experiments in English, Finnish, Mandarin, and random regular languages, we demonstrate that neural language models interpolate between these two forms of generalization: their predictions are well-approximated by a log-linear combination of local and global predictive distributions. We then show that, in some languages, noise mediates the two forms of generalization: noise applied to input tokens encourages global generalization, while noise in history representations encourages local generalization. Finally, we offer a preliminary theoretical explanation of these results by proving that the observed interpolation behavior is expected in log-linear models with a particular feature correlation structure. These results help explain the effectiveness of two popular regularization schemes and show that aspects of sequence model generalization can be understood and controlled.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: Learning Elementary Cellular Automata with Transformers
papers.research_question: Can Transformers learn to abstract and generalize the rules governing Elementary Cellular Automata, and how do they perform in multi-step planning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn and generalize rules of Elementary Cellular Automata, but their planning ability declines without intermediate context; training with future states or rule prediction improves performance, and model depth is crucial for sequential computations.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn and generalize ECA dynamics, but multi-step planning is limited without intermediate context; training strategies that include future states or rule prediction can improve performance, and depth is important for sequential computation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve high accuracy in next-state prediction for ECA and generalize across different Boolean functions.
Performance drops sharply in multi-step planning tasks without intermediate context.
Including future states or rule prediction in the training loss enhances the model's ability to form internal representations of rules, improving planning accuracy.
Model depth scales with the number of steps that can be predicted accurately; more layers are needed for longer planning horizons.
Autoregressive generation performs better than direct multi-step planning, indicating reliance on immediate past states.
papers.limitation:
Performance declines sharply in multi-step planning tasks without intermediate context.
Transformers may struggle to store and propagate state information over multiple steps without explicit intermediate context.
future_direction: Including longer horizons in the loss function for LLMs
Incorporating recurrence for dynamic control
Using adaptive computation time to manage model depth
papers.abstract: Large Language Models demonstrate remarkable mathematical capabilities but at the same time struggle with abstract reasoning and planning. In this study, we explore whether Transformers can learn to abstract and generalize the rules governing Elementary Cellular Automata. By training Transformers on state sequences generated with random initial conditions and local rules, we show that they can generalize across different Boolean functions of fixed arity, effectively abstracting the underlying rules. While the models achieve high accuracy in next-state prediction, their performance declines sharply in multi-step planning tasks without intermediate context. Our analysis reveals that including future states or rule prediction in the training loss enhances the models' ability to form internal representations of the rules, leading to improved performance in longer planning horizons and autoregressive generation. Furthermore, we confirm that increasing the model's depth plays a crucial role in extended sequential computations required for complex reasoning tasks. This highlights the potential to improve LLM with inclusion of longer horizons in loss function, as well as incorporating recurrence and adaptive computation time for dynamic control of model depth.

papers.title: Cognitive Maps in Language Models: A Mechanistic Analysis of Spatial Planning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve spatial navigation tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on exploratory data develop a generalizable cognitive map for spatial navigation, while those trained on goal-directed data learn brittle, path-dependent algorithms, revealing a trade-off between generalization and optimization.
papers.conclusion: Training paradigms shape the algorithms learned by transformers for spatial navigation, with exploratory data encouraging generalizable world models and goal-directed data leading to optimized but brittle heuristics.
papers.key_findings:
The Foraging Model develops a robust, map-like representation of space (cognitive map) and shows a phase transition in layer 8 where it becomes independent of historical direction tokens.
The Foraging Model uses an adaptive strategy: local heuristics for short contexts and map-based reasoning for longer contexts.
The goal-directed SP models learn path-dependent algorithms that remain reliant on explicit directional inputs throughout all layers.
The hybrid SP-RW model improves generalization but retains the path-dependent algorithm of its parent.
Mechanistic analysis reveals a local spatial update circuit in Layer 1 of the Foraging Model and self-sufficient spatial representations from Layer 8 onwards.
papers.limitation:
Use of a simplified 4x4 grid and GPT-2 small architecture limits scalability to more complex environments and larger models.
Mechanistic analysis is incomplete; the exact circuit and transformation of spatial information across intermediate layers remains a black box.
Causal analysis focuses on the Foraging Model, leaving the brittleness of the SP models behaviorally observed but not mechanistically explained.
future_direction: Apply automated circuit discovery techniques to systematically map the transformations of spatial information across intermediate layers.
Prioritize a comparative mechanistic analysis to uncover the algorithmic failures in the SP models.
papers.abstract: How do large language models solve spatial navigation tasks? We investigate this by training GPT-2 models on three spatial learning paradigms in grid environments: passive exploration (Foraging Model- predicting steps in random walks), goal-directed planning (generating optimal shortest paths) on structured Hamiltonian paths (SP-Hamiltonian), and a hybrid model fine-tuned with exploratory data (SP-Random Walk). Using behavioural, representational and mechanistic analyses, we uncover two fundamentally different learned algorithms. The Foraging model develops a robust, map-like representation of space, akin to a 'cognitive map'. Causal interventions reveal that it learns to consolidate spatial information into a self-sufficient coordinate system, evidenced by a sharp phase transition where its reliance on historical direction tokens vanishes by the middle layers of the network. The model also adopts an adaptive, hierarchical reasoning system, switching between a low-level heuristic for short contexts and map-based inference for longer ones. In contrast, the goal-directed models learn a path-dependent algorithm, remaining reliant on explicit directional inputs throughout all layers. The hybrid model, despite demonstrating improved generalisation over its parent, retains the same path-dependent strategy. These findings suggest that the nature of spatial intelligence in transformers may lie on a spectrum, ranging from generalisable world models shaped by exploratory data to heuristics optimised for goal-directed tasks. We provide a mechanistic account of this generalisation-optimisation trade-off and highlight how the choice of training regime influences the strategies that emerge.

papers.title: Predictive Coding or Just Feature Discovery? An Alternative Account of Why Language Models Fit Brain Data
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to embed language representations into a low-dimensional space based on transferability, and shows that this embedding captures the hierarchical organization of language processing in the human brain.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure of language representations reflects the structure of language representations in the human brain, and the method provides a template for investigating relationships between linguistic and cognitive representations.
papers.key_findings:
The representation embedding matrix reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic/semantic tasks, and future word embeddings.
The first dimension of this structure corresponds to a hierarchy from low-level to high-level language processing.
This first dimension maps onto the brain's language processing hierarchy, with early auditory areas explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later model layers.
The representation embeddings can predict which representations best explain brain activity in different regions.
Most pairs of representations are discriminable based on their brain activity patterns, indicating the embeddings capture brain representation structure.
papers.limitation:
The chosen set of representations may not capture the full diversity of the space.
The use of GloVe as the universal input representation may not be truly universal.
The use of linear networks may underestimate relatedness between tasks.
future_direction: Using an even larger number of representations to better map the space.
Using other universal spaces, such as directly using fMRI data as input.
Exploring regularized nonlinear models for the encoder-decoder networks.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have shown that representations drawn from neural network language models are extremely effective at predicting brain responses to natural language. But why do these models work so well? One proposed explanation is that language models and brains are similar because they have the same objective: to predict upcoming words before they are perceived. This explanation is attractive because it lends support to the popular theory of predictive coding. We provide several analyses that cast doubt on this claim. First, we show that the ability to predict future words does not uniquely (or even best) explain why some representations are a better match to the brain than others. Second, we show that within a language model, representations that are best at predicting future words are strictly worse brain models than other representations. Finally, we argue in favor of an alternative explanation for the success of language models in neuroscience: These models are effective at predicting brain responses because they generally capture a wide variety of linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: The Generalization Ridge: Information Flow in Natural Language Generation
papers.research_question: In NLG, how does information evolve across layers during training, and how are different layers of the network functionally organized to support generalization versus memorization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces InfoRidge, an information-theoretic framework, and uses it to reveal a 'generalization ridge' in intermediate layers where predictive information peaks, indicating a trade-off between generalization and memorization.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent generalization ridge in intermediate layers, reflecting a fundamental trade-off between generalization and memorization as information flows deeper into the model.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive information peaks at intermediate layers (the 'generalization ridge') and then declines in final layers.
Incremental information gain is highest in intermediate layers.
Attention patterns show that intermediate layers attend to task-relevant (signal) tokens.
Residual scaling experiments show that under distribution shift, the model relies less on final layers and more on intermediate layers.
The generalization ridge phenomenon persists in multi-token generation scenarios.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in natural language generation (NLG), yet their internal mechanisms for synthesizing task-relevant information remain insufficiently understood. While prior studies suggest that intermediate layers often yield more generalizable representations than final layers, how this generalization ability emerges and propagates across layers during training remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose InfoRidge, an information-theoretic framework, to characterize how predictive information-the mutual information between hidden representations and target outputs-varies across depth during training. Our experiments across various models and datasets reveal a consistent non-monotonic trend: predictive information peaks in intermediate layers-forming a generalization ridge-before declining in final layers, reflecting a transition between generalization and memorization. To further investigate this phenomenon, we conduct a set of complementary analyses that leverage residual scaling, attention pattern, and controlled model capacity to characterize layer-wise functional specialization. We further validate our findings with multiple-token generation experiments, verifying that the observed ridge phenomenon persists across decoding steps. Together, these findings offer new insights into the internal mechanisms of transformers and underscore the critical role of intermediate layers in supporting generalization.

papers.title: Retrieval-Aware Distillation for Transformer-SSM Hybrids
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the performance gap between Transformers and State-Space Models (SSMs) on tasks requiring in-context retrieval by preserving only retrieval-critical attention heads during distillation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces retrieval-aware distillation, a method that preserves only retrieval-critical attention heads when distilling a Transformer into a Transformer-SSM hybrid, achieving comparable performance with far fewer attention heads and significantly reduced memory overhead.
papers.conclusion: Retrieval-aware distillation enables efficient Transformer-SSM hybrids by preserving only retrieval-critical attention heads, closing the performance gap with Transformers at a fraction of the memory cost.
papers.key_findings:
Retaining just 2% of attention heads (10 heads in a 1B model) recovers over 95% of teacher performance on retrieval-heavy tasks.
Retrieval-aware distillation reduces memory usage by 5-6x compared to heuristic hybrid baselines.
Once retrieval is handled by a few attention heads, the SSM backbone can be simplified (e.g., 8x reduction in state dimension) with limited performance loss.
The retrieval functionality remains localized in the preserved attention heads after distillation.
The method outperforms heuristic attention placement strategies that require 10x more attention heads.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on models below 3B parameters, so scalability is unclear.
Head selection relies on a synthetic KV-retrieval probe that may not capture all retrieval settings (e.g., multi-hop retrieval).
Does not enforce KV sharing across layers, which could further reduce memory.
Retrieval is not fully separated from the recurrent backbone; some SSM heads still affect retrieval tasks, limiting how aggressively the state dimension can be reduced.
future_direction: Investigating whether the same small set of heads remains sufficient at larger scale.
Extending the retrieval probe to capture other retrieval settings.
Enabling KV sharing during distillation to further reduce the KV cache.
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) offer efficient sequence modeling but lag behind Transformers on benchmarks that require in-context retrieval. Prior work links this gap to a small set of attention heads, termed Gather-and-Aggregate (G&A), which SSMs struggle to reproduce. We propose *retrieval-aware distillation*, which converts a pretrained Transformer into a hybrid student by preserving only these retrieval-critical heads and distilling the rest into recurrent heads. We identify the essential heads via ablation on a synthetic retrieval task, producing a hybrid with sparse, non-uniform attention placement. We show that preserving **just 2% of attention heads recovers over 95% of teacher performance on retrieval-heavy tasks** (10 heads in a 1B model), requiring far fewer heads than hybrids that retain at least 25%. We further find that large recurrent states often compensate for missing retrieval: once retrieval is handled by these heads, the SSM backbone can be simplified with limited loss, even with an $8\times$ reduction in state dimension. By reducing both the attention cache and the SSM state, the resulting hybrid is $5$--$6\times$ more memory-efficient than comparable hybrids, closing the Transformer--SSM gap at a fraction of the memory cost.

papers.title: Looking Beyond The Top-1: Transformers Determine Top Tokens In Order
papers.research_question: What computation is the Transformer model performing after the saturation event (where the top-1 prediction becomes fixed)?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers determine their top-k output tokens in order of ranking via a discrete task-transition mechanism, a phenomenon intrinsic to the architecture that can be leveraged for improved early-exit strategies and language modeling.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Transformer layers after the top-1 saturation event work on determining lower-ranked tokens in order, proposes a task-transition mechanism underlying this, and shows practical benefits for efficiency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Top-k tokens in Transformers reach saturation (become fixed) sequentially in the order of their final ranking.
This ordered saturation occurs across text, vision, and speech modalities and in untrained models, suggesting it is architecture-inherent.
A simple classifier can predict the current 'task' (which token rank is being determined) from hidden layer embeddings.
Intervening by injecting activations from a saturation layer can causally trigger a transition to the next task.
A novel early-exit strategy based on task transition outperforms existing token-level confidence measures.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not determine which specific components in the Transformer architecture give rise to the ordered saturation phenomenon.
The work does not consider whether the data used was encountered during the models' training.
future_direction: Ablation studies to identify which Transformer components are responsible for the ordered saturation.
Investigating if other DNN architectures (e.g., RNNs) also determine top-k tokens in order.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Transformers is crucial for achieving more accurate and efficient predictions. In this work, we analyze the computation performed by Transformers in the layers after the top-1 prediction has become fixed, which has been previously referred to as the "saturation event". We expand the concept of saturation events for top-k tokens, demonstrating that similar saturation events occur across language, vision, and speech models. We find that these saturation events happen in order of the corresponding tokens' ranking, i.e., the model first decides on the top ranking token, then the second highest ranking token, and so on. This phenomenon seems intrinsic to the Transformer architecture, occurring across different architectural variants (decoder-only, encoder-only, and to a lesser extent full-Transformer), and even in untrained Transformers. We propose an underlying mechanism of task transition for this sequential saturation, where task k corresponds to predicting the k-th most probable token, and the saturation events are in fact discrete transitions between the tasks. In support of this we show that it is possible to predict the current task from hidden layer embedding. Furthermore, using an intervention method we demonstrate that we can cause the model to switch from one task to the next. Finally, leveraging our findings, we introduce a novel token-level early-exit strategy, which surpasses existing methods in balancing performance and efficiency.

papers.title: Systematic Generalization and Emergent Structures in Transformers Trained on Structured Tasks
papers.research_question: How and when can transformers acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization on algorithmic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Two-layer causal transformers with label-based order encoding can learn algorithmic tasks and generalize to longer sequences, exhibiting signs of task decomposition and shared computation across tasks.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve structured algorithmic tasks and generalize systematically, with attention layers developing task decomposition and shared computation.
papers.key_findings:
Label-based order encoding enables strong length generalization in transformers on algorithmic tasks.
Two-layer transformers are sufficient to solve multi-level sorting tasks, while single-layer models fail.
Attention patterns in two-layer models show task decomposition: first layer attends to items in the same feature group, second layer attends to the next output token.
In multi-task learning, transformers can learn multiple tasks simultaneously and generalize to longer sequences, with attention heads showing shared computation across tasks.
Task-conditioned item representations are reorganized according to the task structure, showing clustering by relevant features.
papers.limitation:
Label-based encoding alone would not represent true item distance information.
The tasks are simple and synthetic, and may not capture the complexity of natural data.
future_direction: Explore learning and generalization dynamics in transformer-based agents to understand the acquisition of task-conditioned, multi-level behavioral policies in structured environments.
Characterize the degree of possible computational modularity in multi-headed attention in relation to task structures.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks have seen great success in natural language processing and machine vision, where task objectives such as next word prediction and image classification benefit from nuanced context sensitivity across high-dimensional inputs. However, there is an ongoing debate about how and when transformers can acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization. Here, we explore how well a causal transformer can perform a set of algorithmic tasks, including copying, sorting, and hierarchical compositions of these operations. We demonstrate strong generalization to sequences longer than those used in training by replacing the standard positional encoding typically used in transformers with labels arbitrarily paired with items in the sequence. We search for the layer and head configuration sufficient to solve these tasks, then probe for signs of systematic processing in latent representations and attention patterns. We show that two-layer transformers learn reliable solutions to multi-level problems, develop signs of task decomposition, and encode input items in a way that encourages the exploitation of shared computation across related tasks. These results provide key insights into how attention layers support structured computation both within a task and across multiple tasks.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from The Encoding Specificity Principle
papers.research_question: How do attention layers in transformer-based LLMs implement memory retrieval mechanisms, and are contextual cues represented as keywords?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval, with Q, K, V playing distinct roles analogous to human memory, and that contextual cues are represented as keywords.
papers.conclusion: Attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval mechanisms guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, with keywords serving as retrieval cues and specific neurons encoding these cues.
papers.key_findings:
Swapping V alone induces hallucinations, indicating V stores content.
Swapping both K and V induces systematic hallucination, showing content-addressable matching and content retrieval.
Swapping K only hinders factual recall, representing retrieval failure.
Consistent, model-specific attention neurons are activated by keywords.
Perturbing keywords at the K matrix impairs memory retrieval.
papers.abstract: While explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for large language models (LLMs) remains an evolving field with many unresolved questions, increasing regulatory pressures have spurred interest in its role in ensuring transparency, accountability, and privacy-preserving machine unlearning. Despite recent advances in XAI have provided some insights, the specific role of attention layers in transformer based LLMs remains underexplored. This study investigates the memory mechanisms instantiated by attention layers, drawing on prior research in psychology and computational psycholinguistics that links Transformer attention to cue based retrieval in human memory. In this view, queries encode the retrieval context, keys index candidate memory traces, attention weights quantify cue trace similarity, and values carry the encoded content, jointly enabling the construction of a context representation that precedes and facilitates memory retrieval. Guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, we hypothesize that the cues used in the initial stage of retrieval are instantiated as keywords. We provide converging evidence for this keywords-as-cues hypothesis. In addition, we isolate neurons within attention layers whose activations selectively encode and facilitate the retrieval of context-defining keywords. Consequently, these keywords can be extracted from identified neurons and further contribute to downstream applications such as unlearning.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: How Do Neural Sequence Models Generalize? Local and Global Context Cues\n for Out-of-Distribution Prediction
papers.research_question: How do neural sequence models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts when local and global context cues conflict?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts by interpolating between local and global context cues, and this interpolation can be controlled by noise-based regularization.
papers.conclusion: Neural sequence models' behavior in out-of-distribution contexts can be predicted and is approximated by interpolation of local and global cues, and noise can control this, suggesting avenues for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Neural LMs' out-of-distribution behavior is well approximated by either local or global context models, and best by a log-linear interpolation.
The preference for local vs. global generalization varies across languages (local works better for English and regular languages, global for Finnish and Chinese).
Noise during training can control the interpolation: input noise encourages global generalization, while history noise encourages local generalization.
A theoretical proposition shows that interpolation behavior arises in log-linear models with separate local and global features.
papers.limitation: The theoretical result relies on a feature function that may not realistically represent deep network features, involves strong assumptions, and becomes vacuous for certain parameter values.
future_direction: Explaining data-dependent aspects of the local-global trade-off, especially cross-linguistic differences.
Determining whether architectural improvements can more effectively target specific kinds of structured generalization.
papers.abstract:
After a neural sequence model encounters an unexpected token, can its
behavior be predicted? We show that RNN and transformer language models exhibit
structured, consistent generalization in out-of-distribution contexts. We begin
by introducing two idealized models of generalization in next-word prediction:
a local context model in which generalization is consistent with the last word
observed, and a global context model in which generalization is consistent with
the global structure of the input. In experiments in English, Finnish,
Mandarin, and random regular languages, we demonstrate that neural language
models interpolate between these two forms of generalization: their predictions
are well-approximated by a log-linear combination of local and global
predictive distributions. We then show that, in some languages, noise mediates
the two forms of generalization: noise applied to input tokens encourages
global generalization, while noise in history representations encourages local
generalization. Finally, we offer a preliminary theoretical explanation of
these results by proving that the observed interpolation behavior is expected
in log-linear models with a particular feature correlation structure. These
results help explain the effectiveness of two popular regularization schemes
and show that aspects of sequence model generalization can be understood and
controlled.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Unraveling Token Prediction Refinement and Identifying Essential Layers in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models iteratively refine token predictions through internal processing, and how does the positioning of relevant information within the input context affect this refinement process?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that the depth of token prediction refinement in LLMs, measured by the number of layers between the first correct prediction and its finalization, follows an inverted U-shaped curve relative to the position of relevant information in the input context, with more refinement needed when information is in the middle of long contexts.
papers.conclusion: Investigating intermediate representations using the logit lens provides insights into how LLMs iteratively refine token predictions, which is vital for advancing AI safety research and developing secure, human-aligned AI technologies.
papers.key_findings:
The depth of prediction refinement (layers between initial correct token and final stable output) varies with the position of relevant information, showing an approximately inverted U-shaped curve.
The gap between the layer where the top-1 token first matches the correct answer and where it is finalized is smaller when relevant information is at the beginning or end of the input context.
Not all layers are equally essential for determining final correct outputs; the positioning of relevant information impacts which layers are critical.
The logit lens reveals that early layers produce plausible but inaccurate token predictions, which are gradually refined in middle and later layers.
The model's ability to capture dependency relations and compositional understanding is observed, but may struggle with longer contexts where relevant information is positioned in the middle.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of the logit lens varies significantly depending on the task and model used; for tasks requiring deep, abstract reasoning, layers far from the output may offer little relevant information when analyzed solely through token prediction.
Reducing complex layer representations to token predictions introduces biases, as many layers may serve other functions (e.g., refining internal features or re-weighting contextual information) not captured by logits.
Token distributions can be highly skewed, with some tokens dominating, which may obscure the true purpose or significance of intermediate representations.
The logit lens alone does not fully reveal the layered, nuanced, and abstract processes underlying a language model's true capabilities and must be combined with other techniques for a comprehensive understanding.
papers.abstract: This research aims to unravel how large language models (LLMs) iteratively refine token predictions through internal processing. We utilized a logit lens technique to analyze the model's token predictions derived from intermediate representations. Specifically, we focused on (1) how LLMs access and utilize information from input contexts, and (2) how positioning of relevant information affects the model's token prediction refinement process. On a multi-document question answering task with varying input context lengths, we found that the depth of prediction refinement (defined as the number of intermediate layers an LLM uses to transition from an initial correct token prediction to its final, stable correct output), as a function of the position of relevant information, exhibits an approximately inverted U-shaped curve. We also found that the gap between these two layers, on average, diminishes when relevant information is positioned at the beginning or end of the input context. This suggested that the model requires more refinements when processing longer contexts with relevant information situated in the middle. Furthermore, our findings indicate that not all layers are equally essential for determining final correct outputs. Our analysis provides insights into how token predictions are distributed across different conditions, and establishes important connections to existing hypotheses and previous findings in AI safety research and development.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Probing for Incremental Parse States in Autoregressive Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do autoregressive language models maintain implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures, and do these representations mediate next-word predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive language models learn stack-like representations of incremental syntactic structures that mediate next-word predictions, and these representations can be extracted and intervened upon using probing methods.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive language models learn to maintain and update implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures through pretraining, and these representations can be probed and used to control model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Probes can predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes, indicating that implicit syntactic representations guide next-word predictions.
Probes can causally intervene on model representations to steer model behavior, e.g., making certain syntactic continuations more likely.
The MLP Action Probe (MAP) performs best among the probes, suggesting that stack-based representations are important for incremental parsing in language models.
Autoregressive language models maintain implicit incremental syntactic structures that are dynamically updated during processing.
The geometric probe (GAP) makes strong assumptions about representation geometry and underperforms compared to MAP.
papers.limitation:
The question of what constitutes a probe remains a potential confound.
Counterfactual effects, though significant, are small in absolute terms.
Probes rely on a particular oracle (ArcStandard); other oracles might be better suited.
papers.abstract: Next-word predictions from autoregressive neural language models show remarkable sensitivity to syntax. This work evaluates the extent to which this behavior arises as a result of a learned ability to maintain implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures. We extend work in syntactic probing to the incremental setting and present several probes for extracting incomplete syntactic structure (operationalized through parse states from a stack-based parser) from autoregressive language models. We find that our probes can be used to predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes and causally intervene on model representations and steer model behavior. This suggests implicit incremental syntactic inferences underlie next-word predictions in autoregressive neural language models.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of a Transformer Trained on a Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Task
papers.research_question: How does a transformer internally solve a symbolic multi-step reasoning task, specifically pathfinding in trees? What interpretable mechanisms does it use?
papers.core_contribution: The transformer implements an interpretable backward chaining algorithm for pathfinding, using deduction heads to climb the tree, parallel computation via register tokens, and a one-step lookahead heuristic.
papers.conclusion: The transformer demonstrates deductive reasoning up to a depth bounded by its layers, using parallelized backward chaining and heuristics, suggesting an inductive bias towards parallelized strategies for reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The first layer attention head performs edge token concatenation, copying source node information to target node positions.
Deduction heads in subsequent layers implement backward chaining, climbing the tree one level per layer.
For paths longer than the number of layers, the model uses register tokens to perform parallel backward chaining and merges subpaths.
The model employs a one-step lookahead heuristic that identifies child nodes and increases logits for non-leaf children.
The model's reasoning depth is bounded by the number of layers, beyond which it resorts to heuristics.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is on a synthetic symbolic task, and it is unclear if similar mechanisms exist in large language models trained on natural language.
The analysis is limited to input where the edge list is presented in backward order; other arrangements may lead to different mechanisms.

papers.title: Analyzing Transformer Dynamics as Movement through Embedding Space
papers.research_question: How do the underlying mechanics of Transformer-based language models give rise to intelligent behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes framing Transformer dynamics as movement through embedding space, establishing a 'Theory of Transformers' where intelligent behaviors emerge from the organization of embedding space and the model's composition functions.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a unified framework for understanding Transformers as movement through embedding space, explaining how intelligent behaviors emerge from the organization of embedding space and the dynamics of encoding and decoding walks.
papers.key_findings:
Intelligent behaviors map to paths in Embedding Space which the Transformer random-walks through during inference.
LM training learns a probability distribution over all possible paths, assigning higher probabilities to paths representing intelligent behaviors.
The Transformer is a self-mapping composition function, folding a context sequence into a context-vector such that its proximity to a token-vector reflects co-occurrence and conditioned probability.
Attention contributes a potentially redundant association-bias to the encoding walk, which aggregates features from the context via filtering and aggregation operations.
A three-way correspondence between similarity, association, and angular proximity is established in embedding space, leading to an associative organization.
papers.limitation: Experiments on concept space theory were limited to a single benchmark (Hellaswag) and a few models.
future_direction: Further investigation into the relative impact of vector similarity, position biases, filters, and decoding method across various model flavors.
papers.abstract: Transformer based language models exhibit intelligent behaviors such as understanding natural language, recognizing patterns, acquiring knowledge, reasoning, planning, reflecting and using tools. This paper explores how their underlying mechanics give rise to intelligent behaviors. Towards that end, we propose framing Transformer dynamics as movement through embedding space. Examining Transformers through this perspective reveals key insights, establishing a Theory of Transformers: 1) Intelligent behaviours map to paths in Embedding Space which, the Transformer random-walks through during inferencing. 2) LM training learns a probability distribution over all possible paths. `Intelligence' is learnt by assigning higher probabilities to paths representing intelligent behaviors. No learning can take place in-context; context only narrows the subset of paths sampled during decoding. 5) The Transformer is a self-mapping composition function, folding a context sequence into a context-vector such that it's proximity to a token-vector reflects its co-occurrence and conditioned probability. Thus, the physical arrangement of vectors in Embedding Space determines path probabilities. 6) Context vectors are composed by aggregating features of the sequence's tokens via a process we call the encoding walk. Attention contributes a - potentially redundant - association-bias to this process. 7) This process is comprised of two principal operation types: filtering (data independent) and aggregation (data dependent). This generalization unifies Transformers with other sequence models. Building upon this foundation, we formalize a popular semantic interpretation of embeddings into a ``concept-space theory'' and find some evidence of it's validity.

papers.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
papers.research_question: What mechanisms cause extreme-token phenomena (attention sinks, value-state drains, residual-state peaks) in transformer-based LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the active-dormant mechanism and mutual reinforcement mechanism as the causes of extreme-token phenomena (attention sinks, value-state drains, residual-state peaks) in LLMs, and proposes architectural and optimization modifications to mitigate them.
papers.conclusion: The work uncovers the underlying mechanisms of extreme-token phenomena and suggests potential pathways to mitigate these issues during LLM pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Extreme-token phenomena arise from an active-dormant mechanism in attention heads, where heads become sinks for specific input domains while remaining non-sinks for others.
A mutual reinforcement mechanism between attention sinks and value-state drains drives these phenomena during training.
In pretrained LLMs, many attention heads exhibit a similar active-dormant mechanism as in the simplified Bigram-Backcopy task.
The quantitative properties of extreme-token dynamics in the Bigram-Backcopy task align with observations in pretrained LLMs, including sink-logits concentration.
Replacing softmax with ReLU in attention heads or Adam with SGD can mitigate extreme-token phenomena in the Bigram-Backcopy task.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether eliminating extreme-token phenomena significantly improves downstream tasks like inference and quantization.
future_direction: Explore whether eliminating extreme-token phenomena is essential or beneficial for building powerful transformer-based LLMs.
Pretrain a model at the scale of GPT-2 to study the impact of mitigating extreme-token phenomena.
papers.abstract: Practitioners have consistently observed three puzzling phenomena in transformer-based large language models (LLMs): attention sinks, value-state drains, and residual-state peaks, collectively referred to as extreme-token phenomena. These phenomena are characterized by certain so-called "sink tokens" receiving disproportionately high attention weights, exhibiting significantly smaller value states, and having much larger residual-state norms than those of other tokens. These extreme tokens give rise to various challenges in LLM inference, quantization, and interpretability. We elucidate the mechanisms behind extreme-token phenomena. First, we show that these phenomena arise in very simple architectures -- transformers with one to three layers -- trained on a toy model, the Bigram-Backcopy (BB) task. In this setting, we identify an active-dormant mechanism, where attention heads become sinks for specific input domains while remaining non-sinks for others. Our theoretical analysis of the training dynamics reveals that these phenomena are driven by a mutual reinforcement mechanism. Building on these insights, we propose strategies to mitigate extreme-token phenomena during pretraining, including replacing softmax with ReLU and Adam with SGD. Next, we extend our analysis to pretrained LLMs, including Llama and OLMo, showing that many attention heads exhibit a similar active-dormant mechanism as in the BB task, and that the mutual reinforcement mechanism also governs the emergence of extreme-token phenomena during LLM pretraining. Our results reveal that many of the static and dynamic properties of extreme-token phenomena predicted by the BB task align with observations in pretrained LLMs.

papers.title: How do Transformers perform In-Context Autoregressive Learning?
papers.research_question: How do Transformers perform in-context autoregressive learning? Specifically, how do they estimate the context matrix W in-context and then predict the next token?
papers.core_contribution: The paper characterizes how Transformers perform in-context autoregressive learning, showing that optimally trained linear Transformers implement either gradient descent or geometric relations to estimate the context matrix W in-context.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform in-context autoregressive learning by first estimating the context matrix through gradient descent or geometric relations, with positional encoding playing a crucial role in capturing data structure.
papers.key_findings:
For commuting orthogonal matrices and augmented tokens, a one-layer linear Transformer implements one step of gradient descent on an inner objective as its in-context mapping.
For non-augmented tokens, the global minima of the training loss exhibit orthogonality between heads, and positional encoding captures trigonometric relations in the data.
Experiments show that these findings extend to non-commuting orthogonal matrices.
The distribution of context matrices affects the trained positional encodings, leading to structures resembling traditional positional encodings.
In the augmented setting, multiple layers of linear attention do not outperform gradient descent, whereas a full Transformer with softmax and MLP does.
papers.limitation:
The commutativity assumption for context matrices is strong, and the general non-commutative case is left for future work.
The autoregressive process considered is simplistic and may not fully capture real-world language.
future_direction: Generalizing the analysis to non-commutative context matrices.
Understanding why duplicating data improves performance in the non-augmented setting.
papers.abstract: Transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance in language modeling tasks. However, the reasons behind their tremendous success are still unclear. In this paper, towards a better understanding, we train a Transformer model on a simple next token prediction task, where sequences are generated as a first-order autoregressive process $s_{t+1} = W s_t$. We show how a trained Transformer predicts the next token by first learning $W$ in-context, then applying a prediction mapping. We call the resulting procedure in-context autoregressive learning. More precisely, focusing on commuting orthogonal matrices $W$, we first show that a trained one-layer linear Transformer implements one step of gradient descent for the minimization of an inner objective function, when considering augmented tokens. When the tokens are not augmented, we characterize the global minima of a one-layer diagonal linear multi-head Transformer. Importantly, we exhibit orthogonality between heads and show that positional encoding captures trigonometric relations in the data. On the experimental side, we consider the general case of non-commuting orthogonal matrices and generalize our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study\n with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
papers.research_question: How do the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in deep neural networks under different learning objectives (machine translation, language modeling, masked language modeling)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes to view the evolution of token representations in Transformers from a compression/prediction trade-off perspective, showing that the learning objective (MT, LM, MLM) determines the information flow and the process of losing input information and accumulating output information.
papers.conclusion: The learning objective determines the information flow in the model, and the proposed compression/prediction viewpoint explains the evolution of token representations, relating findings to prior probing task results.
papers.key_findings:
With the LM objective, information about the past gets lost and predictions about the future get formed as you go from bottom to top layers.
For MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity, and then the token identity gets recreated at the top layers.
For MT, representations get refined with context, but most information about the word type does not get lost.
Differences in representations due to training objective are much larger than those due to random initialization.
The analysis provides an explanation for the superior performance of the MLM objective over the LM one for pretraining.
papers.abstract:
We seek to understand how the representations of individual tokens and the
structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in deep neural
networks under different learning objectives. We focus on the Transformers for
our analysis as they have been shown effective on various tasks, including
machine translation (MT), standard left-to-right language models (LM) and
masked language modeling (MLM). Previous work used black-box probing tasks to
show that the representations learned by the Transformer differ significantly
depending on the objective. In this work, we use canonical correlation analysis
and mutual information estimators to study how information flows across
Transformer layers and how this process depends on the choice of learning
objective. For example, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about
the past in left-to-right language models gets vanished and predictions about
the future get formed. In contrast, for MLM, representations initially acquire
information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token
identity and producing a more generalized token representation. The token
identity then gets recreated at the top MLM layers.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: Transformers Are Born Biased: Structural Inductive Biases at Random Initialization and Their Practical Consequences
papers.research_question: Do randomly initialized transformers exhibit systematic structural biases, and what are their mechanisms and practical consequences?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers exhibit strong structural biases at random initialization due to representation contraction driven by MLP and attention, which persist through training and enable seed-specific fingerprinting (SeedPrint) and explain the attention-sink phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are not blank slates; they possess inherent structural biases at initialization that persist through training, with implications for model fingerprinting and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformers show extreme token preferences, with certain tokens predicted orders of magnitude more often than others.
This preference arises from inter-sequence representation contraction, where last-token representations from different sequences become highly similar.
The contraction is primarily driven by asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP layers, and amplified by self-attention through intra-sequence aggregation.
These initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable model identity that can be used for fingerprinting (SeedPrint).
The attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction leads to a positional discrepancy that causally explains the attention-sink phenomenon in trained LLMs.
future_direction: Design architectures that are more neutral or explicitly incorporate desired inductive biases.
Treat initialization choices as hyperparameters tuned for final model behavior, not just optimization stability.
Extend the fingerprinting method to more challenging scenarios, such as detecting obfuscated or distilled models.
papers.abstract: Transformers underpin modern large language models (LLMs) and are commonly assumed to be behaviorally unstructured at random initialization, with all meaningful preferences emerging only through large-scale training. We challenge this assumption by showing that randomly initialized transformers already exhibit strong and systematic structural biases. In particular, untrained models display extreme token preferences: across random input sequences, certain tokens are predicted with probabilities orders of magnitude larger. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon by dissecting the transformer architecture at initialization. We show that extreme token preference arises from a contraction of token representations along a random seed-dependent direction. This contraction is driven by two interacting forces: (i) asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP sublayers induce global (inter-sequence) representation concentration, and (ii) self-attention further amplifies this effect through local (intra-sequence) aggregation. Together, these mechanisms align hidden representations along a direction determined solely by the random initialization, producing highly non-uniform next-token predictions. Beyond mechanistic insight, we demonstrate that these initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable and intrinsic model identity. Leveraging this property, we introduce SeedPrint, a fingerprinting method that can reliably distinguish models that differ only in their random initialization, even after extensive training and under substantial distribution shift.
