(ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Temporal Difference Learning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models implement temporal difference learning to solve reinforcement learning problems in-context, despite being trained only for next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders can reveal and causally manipulate these representations.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders provide a methodology for studying and manipulating these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 3 70B can solve simple reinforcement learning problems in-context and its behavior is best described by a Q-learning model.
Sparse autoencoders trained on the residual stream reveal features that correlate with temporal difference errors and Q-values.
Intervening on these temporal difference features (lesioning or clamping) impairs performance and reduces correlations, demonstrating their causal involvement.
In a grid world task, Llama uses temporal difference-like features to predict the actions of a Q-learning agent.
In a graph learning task, Llama learns global graph structure similarly to the successor representation, and temporal difference features support this learning.
papers.limitation:
The sparse autoencoders are task-specific and not suitable for identifying reinforcement learning variables for arbitrary tasks.
A circuit-level understanding of how these representations come about remains unclear.
The alignment between the model's behavior and the Q-learning agent is not perfect.
future_direction: Build more generic sparse autoencoders for arbitrary tasks.
Replicate findings with different large language models.
Achieve a circuit-level understanding of how temporal difference representations are computed.
Extend the Q-learning model to account for repetition tendencies.
papers.abstract: In-context learning, the ability to adapt based on a few examples in the input prompt, is a ubiquitous feature of large language models (LLMs). However, as LLMs' in-context learning abilities continue to improve, understanding this phenomenon mechanistically becomes increasingly important. In particular, it is not well-understood how LLMs learn to solve specific classes of problems, such as reinforcement learning (RL) problems, in-context. Through three different tasks, we first show that Llama $3$ $70$B can solve simple RL problems in-context. We then analyze the residual stream of Llama using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and find representations that closely match temporal difference (TD) errors. Notably, these representations emerge despite the model only being trained to predict the next token. We verify that these representations are indeed causally involved in the computation of TD errors and $Q$-values by performing carefully designed interventions on them. Taken together, our work establishes a methodology for studying and manipulating in-context learning with SAEs, paving the way for a more mechanistic understanding.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: A Law of Next-Token Prediction in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do contextualized token embeddings evolve across layers in large language models for next-token prediction, and is there a universal pattern?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the law of equi-learning, which states that each layer in a large language model contributes equally to improving next-token prediction accuracy, following an exponential decay pattern.
papers.conclusion: The law of equi-learning provides a quantitative characterization of feature learning in LLMs and offers practical insights for model development, scaling, and interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
The law of equi-learning is consistently observed across a wide range of open-source LLMs, regardless of architecture or pre-training data.
The law emerges after sufficient training and is sensitive to factors like training steps, epochs, and data repetition.
Model scaling analysis reveals that larger models have lower prediction residuals and higher layer-wise decay ratios.
The law is specific to next-token prediction pre-training tasks and does not clearly emerge under masked language modeling or span corruption.
Information flow analysis shows that higher layers increasingly forget past tokens while improving prediction of future tokens.
papers.limitation:
The law is specific to the prediction residual (PR) metric and may not hold for other metrics.
The underlying mechanism driving the equi-learning law is not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding how the decay ratio depends on model depth, pre-training data, and other factors.
Extending the law beyond the PR metric to other evaluation metrics.
Using the law to guide layer-wise learning rates or preserve it during model pruning and fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely employed across various application domains, yet their black-box nature poses significant challenges to understanding how these models process input data internally to make predictions. In this paper, we introduce a precise and quantitative law that governs the learning of contextualized token embeddings through intermediate layers in pre-trained LLMs for next-token prediction. Our findings reveal that each layer contributes equally to enhancing prediction accuracy, from the lowest to the highest layer -- a universal phenomenon observed across a diverse array of open-source LLMs, irrespective of their architectures or pre-training data. We demonstrate that this law offers new perspectives and actionable insights to inform and guide practices in LLM development and applications, including model scaling, pre-training tasks, and interpretation.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: The Geometry of Tokens in Internal Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the geometry of token embeddings and their role in next token prediction within transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a correlation between the intrinsic dimension of token representations and the cross-entropy loss of next token predictions, indicating that prompts with higher loss have tokens lying in higher-dimensional manifolds.
papers.conclusion: The study connects geometric approaches to interpretability by showing that intrinsic dimension of token representations correlates with cross-entropy loss, suggesting ID as a metric for model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Intrinsic dimension of token representations peaks in early to middle layers, with higher peaks for shuffled data.
Cosine similarity among tokens increases with shuffling, indicating greater alignment of token vectors.
Neighborhood overlap shows that structured data retains more coherent token neighborhoods across layers than shuffled data.
There is a statistical correlation between intrinsic dimension and average cross-entropy loss for next token predictions.
The correlation is explained via a relationship between ID of logits and contextual entropy, and through toy models showing log dimension dependence.
papers.limitation:
Observables computed at low ranges of nearest neighbors; multiscale analysis could reveal more.
Differences in distribution patterns for structured vs shuffled data need further investigation.
future_direction: Multiscale analysis of observables.
Investigation of other geometric observables and their relation to next token probabilities.
Applications to design and training of LLMs for interpretability and efficiency.
papers.abstract: We investigate the relationship between the geometry of token embeddings and their role in the next token prediction within transformer models. An important aspect of this connection uses the notion of empirical measure, which encodes the distribution of token point clouds across transformer layers and drives the evolution of token representations in the mean-field interacting picture. We use metrics such as intrinsic dimension, neighborhood overlap, and cosine similarity to observationally probe these empirical measures across layers. To validate our approach, we compare these metrics to a dataset where the tokens are shuffled, which disrupts the syntactic and semantic structure. Our findings reveal a correlation between the geometric properties of token embeddings and the cross-entropy loss of next token predictions, implying that prompts with higher loss values have tokens represented in higher-dimensional spaces.

papers.title: Dynamical Properties of Tokens in Self-Attention and Effects of Positional Encoding
papers.research_question: What are the dynamical properties of tokens in the continuous-time limit of pre-trained Transformer self-attention, and how do different positional encodings affect these dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical analysis of token dynamics in self-attention, deriving conditions under which tokens converge or diverge, and shows that convergence harms model performance. It then proposes simple architectural refinements to mitigate convergence in Transformers with absolute or rotary positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical and empirical analysis of token dynamics provides insights for improving Transformer architectures, and the proposed refinements to positional encoding schemes effectively mitigate harmful convergence behavior.
papers.key_findings:
When the matrix A (defined as W*(V^T)^{-1}) is negative definite and W is positive definite, tokens converge to zero, which negatively impacts model performance.
Absolute positional encoding has minimal effect on token dynamics, while rotary positional encoding encourages token divergence.
Empirical validation on language and vision tasks shows that constraining models to a divergence regime improves performance over baseline and convergence regimes.
In the divergence scenario, tokens organize into a small number of groups, with tokens within the same group diverging to infinity in a consistent direction.
Simple refinements to the query-key interaction matrix in rotary positional encoding can shift the dynamics from convergence to divergence, leading to improved performance.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis omits other token-wise operations such as layer normalization and feed-forward networks, and assumes time-invariant parameters for analytical simplicity.
The continuous-time limit may not fully capture the discrete-layer behavior of practical Transformers, especially when LayerNorm and FFNs are present.
future_direction: Extend the theoretical framework to incorporate layer normalization and feed-forward networks.
Apply the dynamical analysis to other architectures beyond standard Transformers.
Investigate the effects of other positional encoding schemes on token dynamics.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the dynamical properties of tokens in pre-trained Transformer models and explores their application to improving Transformers. To this end, we analyze the dynamical system governing the continuous-time limit of the pre-trained model and characterize the asymptotic behavior of its solutions. Specifically, we characterize when tokens move closer to or farther from one another over time, depending on the model parameters. We provide sufficient conditions, based on these parameters, to identify scenarios where tokens either converge to zero or diverge to infinity. Unlike prior works, our conditions are broader in scope and more applicable to real-world models. Furthermore, we investigate how different forms of positional encoding -- specifically absolute and rotary -- affect these dynamical regimes. Empirical evidence reveals that the convergence scenario adversely impacts model performance. Motivated by these insights, we propose simple refinements to Transformer architectures that mitigate convergence behavior in models with absolute or rotary positional encoding. These findings support theoretical foundations and design principles for improving Transformer models.

papers.title: Finite State Automata Inside Transformers with Chain-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Study on State Tracking
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) help transformers recover a world model in the form of finite state automata (FSAs), or do they merely learn shortcuts?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer+CoT learns implicit finite state automata (FSAs) for state tracking, as evidenced by mechanistic analysis showing that late-layer MLP neurons implement state transitions and exhibit compression and distinction properties.
papers.conclusion: Transformer+CoT achieves near-perfect next-token prediction while internalizing an FSA-like structured state representation, bridging the gap between theoretical expressiveness and practical learnability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer+CoT efficiently learns state tracking for sequences of arbitrary length across multiple groups (Z60, A4 × Z5, A5), outperforming other architectures like RNNs and transformer variants.
The circuit for state tracking relies heavily on late-layer MLP neurons, with MLP11 playing a key role.
Neurons in late-layer MLPs can be classified into states based on transition rules with high accuracy, indicating an N-to-1 mapping between neurons and states.
The model exhibits near-perfect compression and distinction metrics, providing evidence that it recovers an implicit FSA structure.
The learned FSAs are robust to skipping intermediate steps and noise in scratchpads, but struggle with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
papers.limitation: The model struggles with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
future_direction: Modifications to model architecture, loss functions, or optimization algorithms to improve length generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances the performance of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks, and prior research shows that CoT can theoretically increase expressiveness. However, there is limited mechanistic understanding of the algorithms that Transformer+CoT can learn. Our key contributions are: (1) We evaluate the state tracking capabilities of Transformer+CoT and its variants, confirming the effectiveness of CoT. (2) Next, we identify the circuit (a subset of model components, responsible for tracking the world state), indicating that late-layer MLP neurons play a key role. We propose two metrics, compression and distinction, and show that the neuron sets for each state achieve nearly 100% accuracy, providing evidence of an implicit finite state automaton (FSA) embedded within the model. (3) Additionally, we explore three challenging settings: skipping intermediate steps, introducing data noises, and testing length generalization. Our results demonstrate that Transformer+CoT learns robust algorithms (FSAs), highlighting its resilience in challenging scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/IvanChangPKU/FSA.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Latent Positional Information is in the Self-Attention Variance of Transformer Language Models Without Positional Embeddings
papers.research_question: Where is positional information stored in transformer language models without positional embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without positional embeddings inherently encode strong positional information through the shrinkage of self-attention variance, an effect that persists after pre-training.
papers.conclusion: Positional information is encoded in the self-attention variance of transformer language models without positional embeddings, justifying their removal for more efficient pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
The variance of the self-attention output in a randomly initialized transformer language model without positional embeddings decreases as the token position increases, providing latent positional information.
This variance shrinkage effect is attributed to the interaction between the causal attention mask and the transformer architecture.
The derived variance properties for the randomly initialized model are also observed in the lower layers of a fully pre-trained model.
BERT without positional embeddings fails to encode positional information because its bidirectional attention leads to constant variance across all positions.
Predicting the position of later tokens is more challenging due to the plateauing of variance for larger positions.
papers.limitation: The analysis relies on assumptions of a randomly initialized and frozen TLM and randomly sampled input tokens, which do not hold for human languages and pre-trained TLMs.
future_direction: Analyze the training dynamics of a TLM to understand the model parameter distribution after pre-training.
Use Zipf's law or n-gram language models to quantify the degree of input token duplication in human languages for a more accurate variance estimate.
papers.abstract: The use of positional embeddings in transformer language models is widely accepted. However, recent research has called into question the necessity of such embeddings. We further extend this inquiry by demonstrating that a randomly initialized and frozen transformer language model, devoid of positional embeddings, inherently encodes strong positional information through the shrinkage of self-attention variance. To quantify this variance, we derive the underlying distribution of each step within a transformer layer. Through empirical validation using a fully pretrained model, we show that the variance shrinkage effect still persists after extensive gradient updates. Our findings serve to justify the decision to discard positional embeddings and thus facilitate more efficient pretraining of transformer language models.

papers.title: Pool Me Wisely: On the Effect of Pooling in Transformer-Based Models
papers.research_question: How do different pooling strategies affect the expressivity and downstream performance of Transformer-based models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a theoretical framework that characterizes the expressivity of Transformer-based models with different pooling strategies, and provides empirical validation across modalities, offering practical guidance for pooling selection.
papers.conclusion: Pooling is a critical architectural component in Transformer models, and task-specific pooling design is important, as shown by a unified theoretical and empirical perspective.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical bounds show pooling strategies affect expressivity differently: Average pooling contracts by 1/√n, Sum expands by √n, Last-token is neutral, and Max scales with √min(n,d).
Empirical results show no single pooling strategy dominates all tasks; the best choice depends on whether the task requires global or local context.
Average pooling performs well on tasks requiring global context (e.g., inpainting, segmentation), while Last-token pooling is better for tasks needing local context (e.g., next-token prediction).
Learnable pooling methods like Weighted Average can adapt but may underperform in low-resource settings.
The theoretical bounds hold across different attention mechanisms (standard, L2-MHA, LipsFormer).
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, though it extends to multi-layer.
future_direction: Explore adaptive pooling mechanisms that dynamically adjust to input characteristics.
Extend the analysis to other modalities and architectures.
papers.abstract: Transformer models have become the dominant backbone for sequence modeling, leveraging self-attention to produce contextualized token representations. These are typically aggregated into fixed-size vectors via pooling operations for downstream tasks. While much of the literature has focused on attention mechanisms, the role of pooling remains underexplored despite its critical impact on model behavior. In this paper, we introduce a theoretical framework that rigorously characterizes the expressivity of Transformer-based models equipped with widely used pooling methods by deriving closed-form bounds on their representational capacity and the ability to distinguish similar inputs. Our analysis extends to different variations of attention formulations, demonstrating that these bounds hold across diverse architectural variants. We empirically evaluate pooling strategies across tasks requiring both global and local contextual understanding, spanning three major modalities: computer vision, natural language processing, and time-series analysis. Results reveal consistent trends in how pooling choices affect accuracy, sensitivity, and optimization behavior. Our findings unify theoretical and empirical perspectives, providing practical guidance for selecting or designing pooling mechanisms suited to specific tasks. This work positions pooling as a key architectural component in Transformer models and lays the foundation for more principled model design beyond attention alone.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: N-Gram Learning and Pretraining Dynamics in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformer language models acquire capabilities during pretraining, and what is the relationship between n-gram probabilities and this learning process?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation demonstrates a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning during pretraining, showing that language model learning is highly dependent on surface-level statistics and identifies bigram subnetworks as a minimal circuit for next token prediction.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning, suggesting that traditional distributional statistics still play a role in complex transformer models. Bigram subnetworks comprise a minimal subset of parameters necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn words differently from human children; word frequencies (unigram probabilities) account for the vast majority of variance in words' ages of acquisition in language models, but not in children.
Language model learning can be characterized as early n-gram learning for increasing n, followed by gradual refinement of low-probability n-gram predictions based on longer contexts and more nuanced capabilities.
Subnetworks that make bigram predictions exist in fully trained language models and are critical for model performance, even when they consist of less than 0.2% of model parameters.
Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer and overlap significantly with subnetworks trained to optimally prune a given model.
Bigram subnetworks recreate a pattern from the full models where the first layer induces a sharp change that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations.
papers.limitation:
Surprisal is an imperfect proxy for language model learning; a model might achieve the same surprisal at different points using different internal prediction strategies.
The work only considers language models with 124M parameters trained on 5.1B tokens, and learning curves may differ across model sizes.
future_direction: Further research is necessary to determine the effects of model size on learning speed, variability, and forgetting.
Characterize the examples (e.g., based on types of reasoning, world knowledge, or commonsense) that fluctuate at different points during pre-training across model sizes.
Bigram subnetworks can lay a foundation for studying more complex language model circuits by building up from a minimal circuit.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models have received unprecedented attention in recent years due to impressive performance on natural language tasks, but how they acquire these capabilities is largely unknown. During pretraining, language models are trained to predict next tokens (e.g. words) in text, and the field of pretraining dynamics aims to demonstrate how this learning objective leads to consistent learning patterns and mechanisms. The primary contributions of this dissertation are to demonstrate relationships between n-gram probabilities (next token predictions based only on the previous n-1 tokens) and language model learning during pretraining. I first show that language models learn words differently from human children; word frequencies (unigram probabilities) account for the vast majority of variance in words’ ages of acquisition in language models, but not in children. I then characterize language model learning as early n-gram learning for increasing n, then gradual refinement of low probability n-gram predictions based on longer contexts and more nuanced capabilities. Mechanistically, subnetworks that make bigram predictions exist in the models long after the full models have moved on from simple bigram predictions. These bigram subnetworks are critical to language modeling performance even in fully trained models, and they recreate several key properties of a language model’s activation space across layers. Together, these results demonstrate a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning, suggesting that traditional distributional statistics still play some role in these more complex models.

papers.title: If Attention Serves as a Cognitive Model of Human Memory Retrieval, What is the Plausible Memory Representation?
papers.research_question: Investigates whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Transformer Grammar's attention, operating on syntactic structures, better predicts human reading times than vanilla Transformer, suggesting dual memory representations in human sentence processing with attention as a general memory retrieval algorithm.
papers.conclusion: Attention can serve as the general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from two representational systems, and Transformer Grammar, with its syntactic structure-based attention, best captures dominant factors in human sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
TG's NAE has stronger predictive power for reading times than Transformer's NAE.
TG's and Transformer's NAE have independent contributions to reading time prediction, suggesting they capture distinct aspects of memory retrieval.
TG's NAE captures interference effects, independent of decay effects modeled by Category Locality Theory.
TG's advantage over TG−comp indicates the importance of treating closed phrases as single representations (via COMPOSE attention) for capturing syntax-based memory retrieval.
The attention mechanism serves as a general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from dual representational systems (syntactic and token-based).
papers.limitation:
The NAE calculation procedure (summing across heads, handling subwords) strictly followed Oh and Schuler (2022), but alternative approaches warrant investigation.
The findings are based on the English Natural Stories corpus; generalizability to other languages and cognitive measures (e.g., gaze duration, EEG) remains to be investigated.
The use of 'perfect oracles' for syntactic structures idealizes away from local ambiguities that humans encounter during actual sentence processing.
future_direction: Incorporate more realistic elements such as parallel parsing, left-corner parsing strategies, and memory decay mechanisms to fully operate at the algorithmic level.
Investigate generalizability to different languages and other measures of cognitive load.
Explore alternative approaches to handling layers, attention heads, and subword tokens in NAE calculation.
papers.abstract: Recent work in computational psycholinguistics has revealed intriguing parallels between attention mechanisms and human memory retrieval, focusing primarily on vanilla Transformers that operate on token-level representations. However, computational psycholinguistic research has also established that syntactic structures provide compelling explanations for human sentence processing that token-level factors cannot fully account for. In this paper, we investigate whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis between models and humans. Our experiments demonstrate that TG's attention achieves superior predictive power for self-paced reading times compared to vanilla Transformer's, with further analyses revealing independent contributions from both models. These findings suggest that human sentence processing involves dual memory representations -- one based on syntactic structures and another on token sequences -- with attention serving as the general memory retrieval algorithm, while highlighting the importance of incorporating syntactic structures as representational units.

papers.title: How Does BERT Answer Questions? A Layer-Wise Analysis of Transformer Representations
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models, specifically BERT, answer questions? The paper investigates whether Transformers answer questions decompositionally, whether specific layers solve different tasks, how fine-tuning influences the inner state, and whether layer-wise analysis can help understand prediction errors.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's hidden states go through distinct phases (semantic clustering, entity matching, question-fact matching, answer extraction) when answering questions, similar to traditional NLP pipelines. Fine-tuning has minimal impact on semantic abilities, and errors can be detected early in the network.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that hidden states contain interpretable information, revealing phases in BERT's transformations and modularity across layers, which can be used for error analysis and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's hidden states go through four phases: semantic clustering, connecting entities with mentions and attributes, matching questions with supporting facts, and answer extraction.
Fine-tuning has little impact on the model's semantic abilities, as shown by probing tasks.
Prediction errors can be recognized in the vector representations of even early layers.
The positional embedding's effect is maintained even in late layers.
The model's ability to resolve question type is relevant for SQuAD but not for bAbI, and fine-tuning affects this ability accordingly.
future_direction: Development of methods to further process the interpretable information from hidden states.
Investigation of skip connections in Transformer layers for direct information transfer between non-adjacent layers.
Fitting parts of the network to specific tasks in pre-training instead of end-to-end language modeling.
papers.abstract: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) reach state-of-the-art results in a variety of Natural Language Processing tasks. However, understanding of their internal functioning is still insufficient and unsatisfactory. In order to better understand BERT and other Transformer-based models, we present a layer-wise analysis of BERT's hidden states. Unlike previous research, which mainly focuses on explaining Transformer models by their attention weights, we argue that hidden states contain equally valuable information. Specifically, our analysis focuses on models fine-tuned on the task of Question Answering (QA) as an example of a complex downstream task. We inspect how QA models transform token vectors in order to find the correct answer. To this end, we apply a set of general and QA-specific probing tasks that reveal the information stored in each representation layer. Our qualitative analysis of hidden state visualizations provides additional insights into BERT's reasoning process. Our results show that the transformations within BERT go through phases that are related to traditional pipeline tasks. The system can therefore implicitly incorporate task-specific information into its token representations. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that fine-tuning has little impact on the models' semantic abilities and that prediction errors can be recognized in the vector representations of even early layers.

papers.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
papers.research_question: Do transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causal world models, and how are these models structured and used?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks develop causal world models, with interventions revealing an asymmetry (activation easier than suppression) and positional encodings affect the world model structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks form causal world models that capture maze connectivity, and these representations are used for solving.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causally relevant world models.
Interventions that activate features are more effective than those that remove them (asymmetry).
Models can reason about mazes with more simultaneously active features than seen during training, but fail when the same mazes are provided via longer input sequences.
Positional encoding schemes influence how world models are structured (e.g., Stan uses a compositional code, Terry uses single features).
SAEs are better than linear probes for isolating world models.
papers.limitation: Stan was unable to generalize to sequences containing more connections than it had seen during training, leading to failure in removal interventions.
future_direction: Future research could explore how to impose constraints on AI systems in terms of the features they acquire as a result of training.
Future work could investigate how these findings generalize to more complex environments and tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies in interpretability have explored the inner workings of transformer models trained on tasks across various domains, often discovering that these networks naturally develop highly structured representations. When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses. By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them. Furthermore, we find that models can reason about mazes involving more simultaneously active features than they encountered during training; however, when these same mazes (with greater numbers of connections) are provided to models via input tokens instead, the models fail. Finally, we demonstrate that positional encoding schemes appear to influence how World Models are structured within the model's residual stream.

papers.title: Semantic Composition in Visually Grounded Language Models
papers.research_question: This thesis explores whether and how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces multiple methods (WinogroundVQA, Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, Causal Tracing, Syntactic MeanPool, Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization) to probe, analyze, and improve the compositional abilities of visually grounded language models.
papers.conclusion: The work explores the compositionality of visually grounded semantics, introducing methods to probe and improve it, and draws connections to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.
papers.key_findings:
Generative vision-language models like BLIP 2.0 and MiniGPT-4 perform poorly on the compositional WinogroundVQA benchmark.
Syntactic Neural Module Distillation reveals that larger sentence embedding models (GTR-T5) are more compositional, but model size is not the only determining factor.
Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization (CACR) improves relation alignment in vision-language models and outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method (IAIS) on the Winoground benchmark.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute restrictions, hyperparameter tuning for the SynNaMoN experiments was unfeasible, and the dataset had to be constrained to a subset of trees and production rules.
The choice of linguistic formalism (Penn Treebank) may influence the probing results of compositional structure.
future_direction: Exploring whether different linguistic formalisms are better proxies for a model's compositional structure.
Further work on the causal tracing experiment for image captioning models (implementation in progress).
papers.abstract: What is sentence meaning and its ideal representation? Much of the expressive power of human language derives from semantic composition, the mind's ability to represent meaning hierarchically & relationally over constituents. At the same time, much sentential meaning is outside the text and requires grounding in sensory, motor, and experiential modalities to be adequately learned. Although large language models display considerable compositional ability, recent work shows that visually-grounded language models drastically fail to represent compositional structure. In this thesis, we explore whether & how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so. Specifically, we introduce 1) WinogroundVQA, a new compositional visual question answering benchmark, 2) Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, a measure of compositional ability in sentence embedding models, 3) Causal Tracing for Image Captioning Models to locate neural representations vital for vision-language composition, 4) Syntactic MeanPool to inject a compositional inductive bias into sentence embeddings, and 5) Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization, a self-supervised objective function for vision-language relation alignment. We close by discussing connections of our work to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.

papers.title: Planning Transformer: Long-Horizon Offline Reinforcement Learning with Planning Tokens
papers.research_question: How can compounding error in long-horizon offline reinforcement learning be reduced by incorporating high-level planning tokens into a transformer-based model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Planning Tokens, which extend Decision Transformers for offline RL by incorporating high-level planning tokens to reduce compounding error, achieving state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon tasks and improving interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The Planning Transformer framework integrates multi-token planning with transformer-based RL, enhancing long-horizon decision-making and achieving competitive or state-of-the-art performance on D4RL benchmarks while offering interpretability benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Planning Tokens significantly improve performance on long-horizon offline RL tasks, establishing new state-of-the-art results on D4RL benchmarks.
The model outperforms prior RvS methods on goal-conditioned long-horizon benchmarks like Antmaze and FrankaKitchen.
Plans enhance interpretability through visualizations of planned paths and attention maps, providing insights into the model's decision-making.
Ablation studies show that using relative states and projecting the first state to goal space improves performance across environments.
The method is simpler and more flexible than hierarchical RL approaches while maintaining competitive performance in reward-conditioned environments.
papers.limitation: The method may not suffice in non-Markov environments where decisions depend on intricate historical contexts.
future_direction: Extending PT to online learning environments.
Handling non-Markovian environments through temporal encoders.
Applying the framework to other domains such as NLP and large language models.
papers.abstract: Supervised learning approaches to offline reinforcement learning, particularly those utilizing the Decision Transformer, have shown effectiveness in continuous environments and for sparse rewards. However, they often struggle with long-horizon tasks due to the high compounding error of auto-regressive models. To overcome this limitation, we go beyond next-token prediction and introduce Planning Tokens, which contain high-level, long time-scale information about the agent's future. Predicting dual time-scale tokens at regular intervals enables our model to use these long-horizon Planning Tokens as a form of implicit planning to guide its low-level policy and reduce compounding error. This architectural modification significantly enhances performance on long-horizon tasks, establishing a new state-of-the-art in complex D4RL environments. Additionally, we demonstrate that Planning Tokens improve the interpretability of the model's policy through the interpretable plan visualisations and attention map.

papers.title: Tracing and Manipulating intermediate values in Neural Math Problem Solvers
papers.research_question: How are intermediate values of latent structured inputs (specifically arithmetic equations) encoded in a Transformer model's internal representations, and are these encoded features used during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that intermediate values in arithmetic problems are encoded in specific directions of a Transformer model's internal representations and that manipulating activations along these directions causally influences model predictions.
papers.conclusion: The case study shows how manipulations in activation space can find a causal connection to intermediate values, indicating that the model has a locality to certain intermediate values, which is useful for enhancing model interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Principal component analysis (PCA) reveals directions in the model's activation space that are highly correlated with intermediate values of arithmetic equations.
Manipulating model activations along these correlated directions changes the model's predictions in a way consistent with altering the corresponding intermediate value.
Not all directions with high correlation to an intermediate value are causally influential; some are correlated but do not determine model predictions.
The method combines tracing (correlation analysis) and manipulation (causal intervention) to establish a causal link between specific internal representations and model behavior.
papers.abstract: How language models process complex input that requires multiple steps of inference is not well understood. Previous research has shown that information about intermediate values of these inputs can be extracted from the activations of the models, but it is unclear where that information is encoded and whether that information is indeed used during inference. We introduce a method for analyzing how a Transformer model processes these inputs by focusing on simple arithmetic problems and their intermediate values. To trace where information about intermediate values is encoded, we measure the correlation between intermediate values and the activations of the model using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, we perform a causal intervention by manipulating model weights. This intervention shows that the weights identified via tracing are not merely correlated with intermediate values, but causally related to model predictions. Our findings show that the model has a locality to certain intermediate values, and this is useful for enhancing the interpretability of the models.

papers.title: Look Before You Leap: A Universal Emergent Decomposition of Retrieval Tasks in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models internally solve retrieval tasks? Is there a universal modular decomposition across models and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers a universal emergent modular decomposition of retrieval tasks in language models' layers and demonstrates a proof-of-concept application for scalable internal oversight to mitigate prompt injection.
papers.conclusion: The study presents evidence of an emergent decomposition of retrieval tasks across models and tasks, and shows that interpretability can be turned into practical solutions for scalable internal oversight of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Language models decompose retrieval tasks modularly: middle layers at the last token position process the request, while late layers retrieve the correct entity from the context.
Request-patching (residual stream patching at middle layers) allows modular combination of request and context from different inputs, preserving over 70% of the original correct token probability in most model-task pairs.
This decomposition is universal across 18 models (125M to 70B parameters) and six task domains (e.g., question answering, translation, coding).
Fine-grained analysis on Pythia-2.8b shows request processing is distributed across attention heads and MLPs, while retrieval is more localized.
The decomposition enables a proof-of-concept internal oversight method that mitigates prompt injection, improving accuracy from 15.5% to 97.5% on Pythia-12b with human supervision on only a single input.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to retrieval tasks with a simple structure.
The application is a proof of concept limited to a single simple question-answering task.
future_direction: Extending the ORION input structure to include more advanced requests (e.g., more filtering conditions).
Automating dataset creation using frontier LMs like GPT-4 to generate large sets of tasks from problem specifications.
Applying dataset design principles to other types of tasks beyond retrieval.
papers.abstract: When solving challenging problems, language models (LMs) are able to identify relevant information from long and complicated contexts. To study how LMs solve retrieval tasks in diverse situations, we introduce ORION, a collection of structured retrieval tasks spanning six domains, from text understanding to coding. Each task in ORION can be represented abstractly by a request (e.g. a question) that retrieves an attribute (e.g. the character name) from a context (e.g. a story). We apply causal analysis on 18 open-source language models with sizes ranging from 125 million to 70 billion parameters. We find that LMs internally decompose retrieval tasks in a modular way: middle layers at the last token position process the request, while late layers retrieve the correct entity from the context. After causally enforcing this decomposition, models are still able to solve the original task, preserving 70% of the original correct token probability in 98 of the 106 studied model-task pairs. We connect our macroscopic decomposition with a microscopic description by performing a fine-grained case study of a question-answering task on Pythia-2.8b. Building on our high-level understanding, we demonstrate a proof of concept application for scalable internal oversight of LMs to mitigate prompt-injection while requiring human supervision on only a single input. Our solution improves accuracy drastically (from 15.5% to 97.5% on Pythia-12b). This work presents evidence of a universal emergent modular processing of tasks across varied domains and models and is a pioneering effort in applying interpretability for scalable internal oversight of LMs.

papers.title: Mechanics of Next Token Prediction with Self-Attention
papers.research_question: What does a single self-attention layer learn from next-token prediction? The paper shows that training self-attention with gradient descent learns an automaton which generates the next token in two distinct steps: hard retrieval and soft composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that gradient descent on a single-layer self-attention for next-token prediction learns an automaton that performs hard retrieval of high-priority tokens and soft composition, characterized by strongly-connected components of a token-priority graph.
papers.conclusion: The work sheds light on how self-attention processes sequential data and paves the way toward demystifying more complex architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient descent on self-attention for next-token prediction leads to a decomposition of weights into a hard retrieval component and a soft composition component.
The hard retrieval component selects tokens based on strongly-connected components in a token-priority graph derived from data.
Under suitable conditions (log-loss, specific assumptions), the optimization landscape is convex and gradient descent converges globally to the solution of an SVM problem (Graph-SVM).
For acyclic datasets, the implicit bias of self-attention is characterized by an SVM that enforces strict priority orders among tokens.
In more general settings (e.g., with nonconvex head), gradient descent may exhibit local convergence, characterized by pseudo token-priority graphs.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are trained on large datasets to predict the next token given an input sequence. Despite this simple training objective, they have led to revolutionary advances in natural language processing. Underlying this success is the self-attention mechanism. In this work, we ask: $\textit{What}$ $\textit{does}$ $\textit{a}$ $\textit{single}$ $\textit{self-attention}$ $\textit{layer}$ $\textit{learn}$ $\textit{from}$ $\textit{next-token}$ $\textit{prediction?}$ We show that training self-attention with gradient descent learns an automaton which generates the next token in two distinct steps: $\textbf{(1)}$ $\textbf{Hard}$ $\textbf{retrieval:}$ Given input sequence, self-attention precisely selects the $\textit{high-priority}$ $\textit{input}$ $\textit{tokens}$ associated with the last input token. $\textbf{(2)}$ $\textbf{Soft}$ $\textbf{composition:}$ It then creates a convex combination of the high-priority tokens from which the next token can be sampled. Under suitable conditions, we rigorously characterize these mechanics through a directed graph over tokens extracted from the training data. We prove that gradient descent implicitly discovers the strongly-connected components (SCC) of this graph and self-attention learns to retrieve the tokens that belong to the highest-priority SCC available in the context window. Our theory relies on decomposing the model weights into a directional component and a finite component that correspond to hard retrieval and soft composition steps respectively. This also formalizes a related implicit bias formula conjectured in [Tarzanagh et al. 2023]. We hope that these findings shed light on how self-attention processes sequential data and pave the path toward demystifying more complex architectures.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models represent the alternate paths they could take during generation? How do hidden activations correlate with token-level uncertainty and steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden activations in language models correlate with token-level uncertainty and can be used to steer generation and predict future outcome distributions, indicating that models implicitly represent alternate reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: Hidden activations in language models reflect token-level uncertainty and can be used to estimate outcome distributions efficiently, offering a way to understand and control model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
Steering success correlates with token-level uncertainty: models are most steerable when they are least certain about the final answer.
Hidden activations contain information about the model's future outcome distribution, as linear probes on the model's own activations predict outcome distribution better than probes on another model's embeddings.
The dynamics of steering success and outcome distribution are similar, with abrupt changes at the same token positions identified by change point detection.
The correlation between steering success and base outcome probability is moderate (R=0.57) and consistent across examples (average R=0.64).
Linear probes are most predictive in middle layers (layers 6-10) of the model.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost of Forking Paths Analysis is high, requiring millions of tokens to analyze a single base path completion.
Only a handful of examples from three datasets are analyzed due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: When a language model generates text, the selection of individual tokens might lead it down very different reasoning paths, making uncertainty difficult to quantify. In this work, we consider whether reasoning language models represent the alternate paths that they could take during generation. To test this hypothesis, we use hidden activations to control and predict a language model's uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. In our experiments, we find a clear correlation between how uncertain a model is at different tokens, and how easily the model can be steered by controlling its activations. This suggests that activation interventions are most effective when there are alternate paths available to the model -- in other words, when it has not yet committed to a particular final answer. We also find that hidden activations can predict a model's future outcome distribution, demonstrating that models implicitly represent the space of possible paths.

papers.title: VisualPredicator: Learning Abstract World Models with Neuro-Symbolic Predicates for Robot Planning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently learn symbolic abstractions that are both perceptually and logically rich for robot task planning from online interaction with the environment?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neuro-Symbolic Predicates (NSPs), a first-order abstraction language combining symbolic and neural representations, and an online algorithm for inventing such predicates and learning abstract world models for robot planning.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a method for learning abstract world models with Neuro-Symbolic Predicates that enables efficient planning and generalization in robotic tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The NSP approach offers better sample complexity, stronger out-of-distribution generalization, and improved interpretability compared to hierarchical RL, VLM planning, and symbolic predicate invention baselines.
The method can autonomously discover abstractions as effective as those crafted by human experts (oracle baseline).
The extended operator learning algorithm contributes to overall performance, as shown by the ablation study.
papers.limitation: The use of derived predicates is not out-of-box compatible with relaxed planning heuristics like LM-cut, leading to larger node expansions and longer planning times in some domains.
future_direction: Develop a version of LM-cut that is compatible with derived NSPs.
papers.abstract: Broadly intelligent agents should form task-specific abstractions that selectively expose the essential elements of a task, while abstracting away the complexity of the raw sensorimotor space. In this work, we present Neuro-Symbolic Predicates, a first-order abstraction language that combines the strengths of symbolic and neural knowledge representations. We outline an online algorithm for inventing such predicates and learning abstract world models. We compare our approach to hierarchical reinforcement learning, vision-language model planning, and symbolic predicate invention approaches, on both in- and out-of-distribution tasks across five simulated robotic domains. Results show that our approach offers better sample complexity, stronger out-of-distribution generalization, and improved interpretability.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
